[MUJAHID:v1p118#2/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | The witnesses must not refuse when called if they had already witnessed the transaction.
[MUQATIL:2:282#2/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Here “more likely” means more suitable: written evidence is more likely to bring testimony in 5:108 and to comfort the wives in 33:51. | mentions 5:108, 33:51
[MUQATIL:2:282#2/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | An immediate cash trade with no term may go unwritten; sales should be witnessed, but a scribe or witness should not be pressured when occupied if another can be found.
[MUQATIL:2:282#2/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Wronging a scribe or witness is sinful; God commands the parties to fear Him and knows all their deeds.
[MUQATIL:2:282/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | A deferred debt’s amount and due date should be written; a fair scribe writes between buyer and seller without increasing the debtor’s amount or reducing the creditor’s right; scribes were few in Muhammad’s time.
[MUQATIL:2:282/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The debtor must dictate the record, fear God, and omit none of what is owed; the warning against shortchanging also appears in 7:85. | mentions 7:85
[MUQATIL:2:282/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | If the debtor is ignorant, mentally impaired, weak, unable to dictate, or cannot speak, the creditor’s guardian dictates fairly, neither adding nor subtracting.
[MUQATIL:2:282/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The right-holder’s representative dictates for an incapable debtor and must be fair, matching the same no-increase, no-decrease standard imposed on the debtor.
[MUQATIL:2:282/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | For a debt, use two acceptable male witnesses or one man and two women; if one woman forgets, the other reminds her, and a summoned witness should serve when free.
[MUQATIL:2:282/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Do not tire of recording even a small amount through its due date: writing better records the term and protects property, is just, reliable for testimony, and less likely to create doubt.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nisba from ʿAdī, Ghanī, Quṣayy, and Umayyah uses wāw to avoid four consecutive yāʾs, deleting the extra yāʾ as in Sulaym and Thaqīf.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nisba from taḥiyyah becomes taḥwī, deleting the yāʾ most like the deleted element in ʿAdī; similar forms follow it.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Qusī and thudī yield qaswī and thadwī because they are fuʿūl forms; when the following kasra disappears, the original pattern returns.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With marma and marmawwiyyah, delete the first two yāʾs and keep the nisba yāʾs; those saying ḥānawī also say marmwī.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus reports that some Arabs retain the yāʾ in Umayyī, analogizing to Ṭayyiʾī; ʿAdiyyī is heavier because of the kasra among yāʾs.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nisba from ḥayyah becomes ḥayawī to avoid consecutive yāʾs; the yāʾ is vocalized so wāw can remain after it.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The tribal name Ḥayy ibn Bahdalah supplies evidence for ḥayawī and for vocalizing yāʾ before wāw.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nisba from layyah becomes lawawī by restoring the underlying form after moving yāʾ; speakers who say Umayyī also say ḥayyī.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr used ḥayyī and layyī, including layyah from the phrase for twisting someone's hand.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nisba from ʿaduww and kuwwah remains ʿaduwwī and kuwwī because there are not enough consecutive yāʾs to require substitution.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Marmawī is analogized to bakhtī because its ending has the same sequence of yāʾs and kasra; maghzawī keeps its form when no cluster arises.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىفعيلوفعيلمنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءات#560/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nisba from ʿadwah becomes ʿadawī because the feminine tāʾ triggers the same treatment as in shanrah/shanʾī.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيف)#800/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Gemination is heavy, so Arabic favors distinct consonants and assimilation into one tongue movement; when the final consonant is quiescent, Hijaz preserves the form while Tamim quiesces the first and vowels the second.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيف)#800/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The form radd stays unassimilated in faʿala because quiescing the ending would still leave gemination, while the first radical is inherently quiescent.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيف)#800/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nouns longer than three letters follow doubled-consonant rules of four-letter verbs: shift a vowel onto a preceding quiescent consonant, retain an existing vowel, and leave preceding alif unchanged; afʿal forms assimilate too.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيف)#800/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A dual nūn can drop and therefore differs from the inseparable doubled consonant after alif; separated doubled consonants do not undergo the same alteration.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيف)#800/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil analyzes ṣabb as faʿala, supported by ṣababtu and ṣabāba, parallel to qaniʿa and qanāʿa.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيف)#800/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms such as ṭabb and khāf follow the three-letter verbal pattern; the lack of an unassimilated tabbab confirms that faʿal is assimilated.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيف)#800/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Three-letter nominals distinguish themselves from verbal forms: weak-verb-like nouns can retain original forms, other nonverbs preserve doubled patterns, and some simplify, as in ʿamīma to ʿamm and thunā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيف)#800/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · قوم | reports | Some speakers preserve the unassimilated faʿil form, as in ḍafaf, because this pattern can be sound in the qult class.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيف)#800/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | Sībawayh prefers ḍaff and ḍafū al-ḥāl over the reported ḍafaf and ḍafafū.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Frequent use of medial wāw and yāʾ led speakers to shift their vowel to the preceding radical, contract the weak letter, and avoid retaining the sound pattern of an unchanged strong verb.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو الخطاب | reports | Abū al-Khaṭṭāb reports dialectal كيد and ما زيل for كاد and زال; speakers shift the vowel as in the passive patterns rather than restore the original vowel.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When these verbs take first-person plural or plural endings, dialects retain kasra or ḍamma and delete the weak letter at the meeting of two sukūns; some use rounding or imāla to signal the deleted yāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | مِتُّ and كِدتُ weaken directly from فعل يفعل rather than through the shifted pattern of قلت and زدت; they are exceptional against the common paradigms.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ليس is treated as a fixed, minimally inflected form: its lack of an imperfect, participle, verbal noun, and productive derivation accounts for its distinctive contraction.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | عور يعور, حول يحول, and صيد يصيد retain their original pattern because their meanings correspond to forms that must preserve the weak radical, such as اعوررت and ابيضضت.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl derives طاح يطيح and تاه يتيه from a wāw-root فعل يفعل pattern, supported by طوحت and توهت; some speakers instead analogize طيحت and تيهت to باع يبيع.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The weak-letter changes in طاح and تاه reflect the frequency of wāw and yāʾ: deletion and sukun avoid accumulating their heavy vowel combinations.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | قُلْتُ is analyzed as a shifted hollow form originally on فعلت; its imperfect يقول confirms the pattern, and Arabic has no corresponding فعلته form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | طُلْتُ belongs to فعلت, as طويل and طوال show; this analysis keeps it intransitive.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعضهم | reports | Some speakers analyze طلت like قلت as a shifted فعلت form; on that analysis طلت becomes transitive, unlike the author's preferred account.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The ya-root forms retain kasra: yāʾ is lighter than wāw, and shifting the light yāʾ into a heavier wāw pattern would be avoided.

فيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | بعتُ is derived through a shifted فعلت pattern, yielding the imperfect يبيع; the shifted pattern governs the imperfect as well as the perfect.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The imperfects يقول and يبيع follow the paradigms to which their perfects were shifted, while يخاف and يهاب remain on their original فعل يفعل pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms such as يخاف and يهاب differ from يزيد and يبيع because the former weakened in their original pattern rather than after being shifted into another one.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In passive forms such as خيف and بيع the basic vowel is kasra; some speakers signal that form with imāla, while other u-vowel pronunciations are secondary assimilations.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | At pause, hāʾ can make audible the final vowel on noninflectional dual and plural nūns, whose preceding consonant is still; the examples include ضاربانه and مسلمونه.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The same pause hāʾ appears in أينه and ثمه because their nūn or final consonant is uninflected, preceded by a still consonant, and phonetically hidden; هلمه is another example.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Many Arab speakers do not add hāʾ at pause when no segment has been deleted; whenever it is added, it disappears before continuing speech.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Similar forms include إنه for إن, اعلمنه with an extra noninflectional nūn, and كيفه, ليته, and لعله; their endings are treated alike in pause.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl reports انطلقته for انطلقت because its tāʾ is not an inflectional ending and is preceded by a still consonant.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Possessive yāʾ suffixes after alif or yāʾ also take pause hāʾ, since the yāʾ is hidden and follows a still consonant, as in غلامايه and عصايه.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An alif inclines toward imāla when followed by kasra, drawing pronunciation toward yāʾ for ease.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In roots with underlying yāʾ, an open alif is inclined because it occupies the place of yāʾ or replaces it.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الفرزدق | reports | Al-Farazdaq's verse with yashumm supports the yāʾ-directed pronunciation used as evidence for imāla.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In wāw roots, imāla follows because final wāw turns to yāʾ after three letters, whereas yāʾ does not turn to wāw; yāʾ is lighter.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some preserve the wāw quality and avoid imāla in short three-letter wāw-root nouns such as qafā, ʿaṣā, and al-qaṭā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Verb alifs from wāw roots incline consistently because the final consonant changes toward yāʾ across inflection; nouns do not undergo that same change.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Many speakers, including many Tamimis, leave open the alif of four-or-more-letter nouns from wāw roots.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An added final alif is often inclined because it behaves like the alif of a yāʾ-root.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Many speakers leave the feminine or other added final alif open, saying ḥublā and maʿzā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some Hijazis incline alif in weak-root forms when the first vowel of faʿaltu is kasra; ordinary speakers do not.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · ابن أبي إسحاق | reports | Ibn Abī Isḥāq reportedly heard Kathīr ʿAzzah say ṣāra; some recited khāfa with imāla, illustrating the restricted middle-wāw case.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Imāla is an articulatory approximation, like moving ṣād toward zāy in ṣadr to ease the tongue's movement.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With medial wāw, imāla is limited to forms beginning with kasra; qāma and dāra do not incline.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some say māta while others say mittu; speakers who say ṣāra and khāfa also use this variation.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The alif in kiyāl and bayyāʿ is inclined because a preceding yāʾ functions like a kasra; many Arabs leave it open.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Speakers who do not incline kiyāl also leave open shaybān, Qays ʿAylān, and Ghaylān, while others incline them for the yāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In a genitive position, some incline alif as in bābihi and mālihi by analogy with kātib and sājid, but the imāla is weaker because the kasra is not fixed.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some extend imāla to accusative zaydan by analogy with Ghaylān, but it is weaker; they do not incline ʿabdan or kaslān because those lack yāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some incline qazḥan and ʿalaman by treating their kasra as though it were yāʾ, and use the same analogy for al-najjādain.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | In genitive forms such as ʿajlānik and mālin kathīr, speakers incline by analogy with bābik and with māshin and dāʿin.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r28] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Speakers differ at pause: some keep imāla, while others open the alif because pausing removes the supporting kasra.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r29] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some incline ʿimādan by analogy with imāla after kasra, while others keep ʿalaman and ʿimādan open without preceding yāʾ or kasra.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A single intervening mobile consonant does not block imāla from an initial kasra, as in ʿimād.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r30] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some pause with bimālin min ʿindi llāh or li-Zaydin māl, analogizing to ʿimād; this is weaker than a connected kasra.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r31] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | They do not say dhā māl this way because a medial alif resembles that of fāʿil; in ʿimādan the second alif follows the first in imāla.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r32] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The second alif in ʿimādan is inclined by the imāla of the first.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In longer nouns from a wāw root, the final alif may incline toward yāʾ once the form has developed a yāʾ, the relevant pattern for musammā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Two intervening consonants still permit imāla when the first is quiescent, since a sākin is a weak barrier.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أهل الحجاز | reports | Hijazis do not apply imāla to the described forms such as sirbāl, shamāl, ʿimād, and kilāb.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | No imāla occurs when the following vowel is fatḥa or ḍamma: fatḥa is closer to alif, while rounding toward wāw would change the letter.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A preceding fatḥa or ḍamma also prevents imāla, as in ribāb, jimād, and al-balbāl.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some incline the alif of as-siwidād because widād behaves like kilāb, a form that accepts imāla.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Hamzat al-waṣl is prefixed so speech can begin before a quiescent consonant; it is an added, vowelled onset.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Sībawayh reports Yunus's account that some speakers say īm Allāh with kasra, then līm Allāh by analogy with the waṣl in ibn.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Waṣl occurs in imperatives of form I when the next consonant is quiescent, in forms such as infaʿala, ifʿalla, and iftaʿala, and in five further derived patterns including istafʿala.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The alif in afʿala is formative rather than an added onset for a quiescent consonant, so its conjugation behaves like a four-letter verb.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A waṣl alif drops after preceding speech because earlier words remove the need for an onset; Sībawayh compares this to dropping hāʾ in vocative speech.

دمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | At the start of speech, waṣl is normally kasra but takes ḍamma when the third letter has ḍamma.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh cites al-Nuʿmān b. Bashīr's line as a poetic example following the rule for adjusting vowels together.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Alif-lām identifies nouns and behaves like qad or sawfa; Ghaylan's line uses bi-dhal and bi-jal, and Sībawayh says the lām is not broken once the form is complete.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil treats the article as separable like qad and sawfa but meaningful; its initial fatḥa distinguishes it, and it remains before an interrogative alif to distinguish question from statement.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An unnamed poet's līman Allāh attests the connected onset in the oath expression.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايجريفيهبعضماذكرناإذاكسرللجمععلىالأصل)#785/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Broken plurals on the fiʿāl pattern can yield expanded forms such as diyāwīr and qiyāwīm.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايجريفيهبعضماذكرناإذاكسرللجمععلىالأصل)#785/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ʿAwār forms ʿawāwīr without hamza, unlike the hamza-bearing pattern; its morphology follows a different base form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايجريفيهبعضماذكرناإذاكسرللجمععلىالأصل)#785/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Weak yāʾ and wāw immediately after alif are treated as word-final radicals, like in siqāʾ and qiḍāʾ; an intervening consonant restores the regular form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايجريفيهبعضماذكرناإذاكسرللجمععلىالأصل)#785/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When separation from the word ending preserves the weak radical, forms such as al-shaqāwa and al-ghiwāya retain the underlying wāw or yāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايجريفيهبعضماذكرناإذاكسرللجمععلىالأصل)#785/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The farther weak radicals stand from the word end, the stronger preservation of the base: zawwār and ṣawwām retain wāw, as do akhwa and abwa.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Plural patterns such as masājid and mafātīḥ resist further broken pluralization as endpoint patterns; as male names they take sound masculine plurals and as female names sound feminine plurals.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Plural patterns that already have broken plural forms can be broken again as names: examples include aʿdāl to aʿādīl and aqwāl to aqāwīl, alongside abyāt, anʿām, and ajriba.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A plural-derived name such as aʿbud can take both a diminutive and a broken plural, yielding al-aʿābid, because its pattern permits these processes like a singular.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A three-consonant plural pattern used as a name follows the broken plural expected of a singular with that form, since it can shift into singular-like patterns and diminutives.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A man named on the fuʿūl pattern may form faʿāʾil, since fuʿūl can also be singular and behaves like an existing plural pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A man named Jamāl on a pattern like singular jirāb takes the broken plural expected of a singular of that form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Tamra used as a name has shifted from its original meaning and behaves like qaṣʿa, allowing tamār just as qaṣʿa allows qiṣāʿ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A following kasra on ر can make a preceding open vowel incline toward kasra: the ر is like two kasra-bearing consonants, so Sibawayh analogizes its effect to ي.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Imala is blocked when an open vowel follows the alif or when an emphatic consonant resists it, as in المحاذر and حاضر.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With ابن مذعور, the speaker approaches kasra after ر but does not incline the و, since it does not resemble ي and tilting it would also tilt what precedes.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A following separate word with ر and kasra can cause imala across the word boundary, as in خبط رياح and قفا رياح.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Other speakers leave forms uninclined when the conditioning kasra is too far away across a word boundary, as in مال قاسم, خبط رياح, and قفا رياح.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some speakers incline before ر in من عمرو but not من الشرق because the latter ر is followed by an emphatic consonant; this also blocks the pattern in مارق.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A doubled verb has two identical consonants at its end, as in رددت and وددت; this is the morphological class of the verse's مضارّ form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | When both final consonants are vowelled, Arabs agree on assimilation; al-Khalil says it is especially apt because repeating the same articulation is burdensome.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أهل الحجاز | reports | The Hijaz dialect keeps the doubled consonants separate when the verb ending is quiescent, moving the preceding consonant to avoid two sukūns together.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بنو تميم | reports | Banu Tamim assimilate the jussive as well as fully vowelled forms; Sibawayh says many other Arabs share this dialect pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If the consonant before the first of the doubled pair is quiescent, it takes that consonant’s vowel; a now-unneeded alif of connection is deleted.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With an alif before the doubled consonants and no alif of connection, the form remains unchanged; لا تضار is one of Sibawayh’s examples.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In ‘إني مما أفعل,’ ما can combine with من as one unit, as in ربما; Abū Ḥayya al-Numayrī’s line illustrates ربما.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nouns such as أهل and مخافة can be annexed directly to an أن-clause, with the sense of أهل لأن يفعل and مخافة لأن يفعل.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some Arabs say ‘لحق أنه ذاهب’ to mean ‘يقين أنه ذاهب,’ but this usage is not common to all Arabs.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | خليق accepts either لأن يفعل or أن يفعل; عسيت أن تفعل similarly follows near-approach verbs such as قاربت and دنوت.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | عسى and اخلولقت take an أن-clause without a verbal-noun alternative here; Arabs do not say ‘عسيت الفعل’ or ‘عسيت للفعل.’
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | عسى is usually invariant across singular, plural, and feminine subjects, though some Arabs inflect it; with inflected forms, أن is accusative as in عسيت أن.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some Arabs use عسى يفعل like كاد يفعل, with a finite verb replacing the accusative noun in the proverb ‘عسى الغوير أبؤسا’; poetry attests this use.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | كاد and كرب normally take a finite verb without أن; poetry permits كاد أن by analogy with عسى, and لعل أن by analogy with عسيت أن.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | يوشك أن تجيء attaches أن to يوشك; توشك أن تجيء is like قاربت أن تفعل, while poetry also uses يوشك يجيء by analogy with عسى.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In ‘أن تضل إحداهما,’ the preposition is omitted; the clause is treated like a verbal noun, as if it said ‘لأن تضل إحداهما.’
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl explains al-Farazdaq’s ‘إن أذنا قتيبة حزتا’ by avoiding separation of أن from its verb, as with كي; it follows إن, which permits nouns before verbs.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After temporal بعد, أن plus a verb stands for a verbal noun; likewise ‘أما أن أسير’ means ‘أما السيرورة.’
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ‘ما منعك أن تأتينا’ means ‘what prevented you from coming to us’: من is omitted before the أن-clause.

r | holds | In ‘إني مما أن أفعل ذاك,’ ما stands for الأمر or الشأن: ‘it is a matter that I do that.’
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ‘بعد ما تقول ذاك القول’ means ‘بعد قولك’; inserting من in ‘من بعد ما’ shows that بعد and ما are not one word.
[SIBAWAYH:إذابنىعلىماقبلهوبمنزلتهفيالاحتياجإلىالحشوويكوننكرةبمنزلة#247/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil allows من and ما here to be indefinite common nouns like إنسان and شيء, with what follows functioning as an adjective.
[SIBAWAYH:إذابنىعلىماقبلهوبمنزلتهفيالاحتياجإلىالحشوويكوننكرةبمنزلة#247/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | هذا من منطلق is awkward when منطلق is a complement or adjective, but longer wording such as من خير منك works; al-Khalil heard Arabs say ما أنا بالذي قائل لك سوءا.
[SIBAWAYH:إذابنىعلىماقبلهوبمنزلتهفيالاحتياجإلىالحشوويكوننكرةبمنزلة#247/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil reports hearing an Arab say ما أنا بالذي قائل لك سوءا and ما أنا بالذي قائل لك قبيحا, showing a descriptive complement after الذي.
[SIBAWAYH:إذابنىعلىماقبلهوبمنزلتهفيالاحتياجإلىالحشوويكوننكرةبمنزلة#247/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In the alternate construction, من and ما serve as relative forms that require a following complement; the words are not intended to stand empty of either complement or description.
[SIBAWAYH:إذابنىعلىماقبلهوبمنزلتهفيالاحتياجإلىالحشوويكوننكرةبمنزلة#247/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When the following material is a relative complement, من and ما are definite, like الذي; the source applies this rule to the dependent clause after الذي.
[SIBAWAYH:إذابنىعلىماقبلهوبمنزلتهفيالاحتياجإلىالحشوويكوننكرةبمنزلة#247/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In هذا من أعرف منطلق, أعرف is an adjective; in هذا من أعرف منطلقا it is a relative complement, while منطلق can also be a predicate as in هذا عبد الله منطلق.
[SIBAWAYH:إذابنىعلىماقبلهوبمنزلتهفيالاحتياجإلىالحشوويكوننكرةبمنزلة#247/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | يا أيها is a means of reaching a noun with the definite article, and الرجل describes أيها; the phrase cannot stop at يا أيها alone.
[SIBAWAYH:إذابنىعلىماقبلهوبمنزلتهفيالاحتياجإلىالحشوويكوننكرةبمنزلة#247/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In الجماء الغفير, الغفير is a required descriptive emphasis, illustrating how a noun can need its descriptor to complete the expression.
[SIBAWAYH:إذابنىعلىماقبلهوبمنزلتهفيالاحتياجإلىالحشوويكوننكرةبمنزلة#247/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The construction رب من supports taking من as indefinite because what follows رب is always indefinite; Amr ibn Qumai'a, Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, and other poets provide examples.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An annexed noun used as a vocative is accusative by an unspoken verb; the singular vocative is nominative in form but occupies an accusative position.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus says the meaning is the same in the nominative and accusative, supporting the accusative adjective analysis.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An annexed adjective of a vocative should be accusative whenever the corresponding singular adjective is accusative.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ya akhānā Zaydan is coordinated with the preceding accusative; Yūnus reports Abu ʿAmr and Medina speakers also say ya akhānā Zayd.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو عمرو | reports | Yūnus reports that Abū ʿAmr and the people of Medina say ya akhānā Zayd, treating the adjective like a standalone vocative.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ya akhānā Zaydan is more common because speakers restore the original accusative after the name leaves the vocative position.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A standalone singular vocative is raised without tanwīn because frequent use led speakers to shorten it and treat it like an interjection.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr says ya Zayd Zayd al-ṭawīlu, repeating the name in a construction explained like ya Zayd al-ṭawīlu.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus reports that Ruʾbah used the accusative repetition ya Zayd Zaydan al-ṭawīlu.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · رؤبة | reports | Ruʾbah's verse ya Naṣru Naṣran Naṣran supports the accusative appositional repetition; Abū ʿAmr's form restarts the vocative.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The adjective of a standalone vocative differs from that of amsi because nominative marking is consistent across vocatives.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl says annexed vocatives and long indefinite calls such as ya rajulan ṣāliḥan are accusative.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some recite ya Naṣru Naṣru Naṣran, retaining a raised second name before the final accusative form.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Coordination such as ya Zayd wa-ʿAmr shares the vocative particle across names; the second name is not an adjective.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl explains accusative al-Naḍr in ya Zayd wa-l-Naḍra as restoration to the underlying case.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Most Arabs whom Sībawayh observed say ya Zayd wa-l-Naḍru with the second name raised.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl treats ya ʿAmru wa-l-Ḥārith as though ya were repeated; a definite noun with alif-lām cannot itself be directly called by ya.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl argues that accusative al-Naḍr would wrongly license accusative sakhlihā in kullu naʿjatin wa-sakhlihā, though its case comes from an understood preposition.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl says raising the coordinated definite noun treats it as wa-Nuḍr; conjunctions share the first element's syntactic governance.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r28] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A coordinated element that follows later enters the same syntactic relation as the first; direct adjacency can prevent the intended indefinite reading.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r29] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The verse's ya ayyuhā address follows the construction illustrated by ya ayyuha al-rajulu; a coordinated name remains carried by ya.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A standalone singular vocative is raised like qablu and baʿdu, though it occupies an accusative position.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r30] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · رؤبة | reports | Ruʾbah's ya dāra ʿAfrāʾ wa-dāra al-bakhdani is poetic evidence that a coordinated phrase remains carried by ya.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r31] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ya hādhā dhā al-jummati has the same construction as ya Zayd dhā al-jummati, with no disagreement.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl allows ya Zayd al-ṭawīlu to be accusative as an adjective of an accusative or as an understood aʿnī, “I mean.”
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl also allows the adjective to be nominative as an adjective of the raised vocative.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl explains the nominative adjective by the consistent nominative marking of every isolated vocative, unlike nouns in amsi al-aḥdathu.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | An adjective that is itself annexed follows the accusative of its vocative; raising it as a standalone vocative would be ungrammatical.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl says ya Zayd nafsahu, ya Tamīm kullakum, and ya Qays kullahum are accusative, like ya Zayd dhā al-jummati.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنالنداءكلاسممضاففيهفهونصبعلىإضمارالفعلالمتروك#287/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | With ya Tamīm ajmaʿūn, either nominative or accusative is possible; accusative cannot be an aʿnī construction.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنحتىتنصبعلىوجهينPageV03P016فأحدهماأنتجعلالدخولغاية#471/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl explains subjunctive حتى as marking a destination: the verb is subjunctive when it is the endpoint, just as a noun is genitive after the corresponding preposition.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنحتىتنصبعلىوجهينPageV03P016فأحدهماأنتجعلالدخولغاية#471/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | حتى also takes a subjunctive when it expresses purpose, like كي with an implicit أن, as in speaking to some

فيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | بعتُ is derived through a shifted فعلت pattern, yielding the imperfect يبيع; the shifted pattern governs the imperfect as well as the perfect.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The imperfects يقول and يبيع follow the paradigms to which their perfects were shifted, while يخاف and يهاب remain on their original فعل يفعل pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms such as يخاف and يهاب differ from يزيد and يبيع because the former weakened in their original pattern rather than after being shifted into another one.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماالياءوالواوفيهثانيةوهمافيموضعالعينمنه)#775/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In passive forms such as خيف and بيع the basic vowel is kasra; some speakers signal that form with imāla, while other u-vowel pronunciations are secondary assimilations.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | At pause, hāʾ can make audible the final vowel on noninflectional dual and plural nūns, whose preceding consonant is still; the examples include ضاربانه and مسلمونه.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The same pause hāʾ appears in أينه and ثمه because their nūn or final consonant is uninflected, preceded by a still consonant, and phonetically hidden; هلمه is another example.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Many Arab speakers do not add hāʾ at pause when no segment has been deleted; whenever it is added, it disappears before continuing speech.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Similar forms include إنه for إن, اعلمنه with an extra noninflectional nūn, and كيفه, ليته, and لعله; their endings are treated alike in pause.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl reports انطلقته for انطلقت because its tāʾ is not an inflectional ending and is preceded by a still consonant.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتلحقهالهاءلتبينالحركةمنغيرماذكرنامنبناتالياء#730/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Possessive yāʾ suffixes after alif or yāʾ also take pause hāʾ, since the yāʾ is hidden and follows a still consonant, as in غلامايه and عصايه.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An alif inclines toward imāla when followed by kasra, drawing pronunciation toward yāʾ for ease.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In roots with underlying yāʾ, an open alif is inclined because it occupies the place of yāʾ or replaces it.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الفرزدق | reports | Al-Farazdaq's verse with yashumm supports the yāʾ-directed pronunciation used as evidence for imāla.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In wāw roots, imāla follows because final wāw turns to yāʾ after three letters, whereas yāʾ does not turn to wāw; yāʾ is lighter.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some preserve the wāw quality and avoid imāla in short three-letter wāw-root nouns such as qafā, ʿaṣā, and al-qaṭā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Verb alifs from wāw roots incline consistently because the final consonant changes toward yāʾ across inflection; nouns do not undergo that same change.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Many speakers, including many Tamimis, leave open the alif of four-or-more-letter nouns from wāw roots.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An added final alif is often inclined because it behaves like the alif of a yāʾ-root.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Many speakers leave the feminine or other added final alif open, saying ḥublā and maʿzā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some Hijazis incline alif in weak-root forms when the first vowel of faʿaltu is kasra; ordinary speakers do not.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · ابن أبي إسحاق | reports | Ibn Abī Isḥāq reportedly heard Kathīr ʿAzzah say ṣāra; some recited khāfa with imāla, illustrating the restricted middle-wāw case.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Imāla is an articulatory approximation, like moving ṣād toward zāy in ṣadr to ease the tongue's movement.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With medial wāw, imāla is limited to forms beginning with kasra; qāma and dāra do not incline.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some say māta while others say mittu; speakers who say ṣāra and khāfa also use this variation.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The alif in kiyāl and bayyāʿ is inclined because a preceding yāʾ functions like a kasra; many Arabs leave it open.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Speakers who do not incline kiyāl also leave open shaybān, Qays ʿAylān, and Ghaylān, while others incline them for the yāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In a genitive position, some incline alif as in bābihi and mālihi by analogy with kātib and sājid, but the imāla is weaker because the kasra is not fixed.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some extend imāla to accusative zaydan by analogy with Ghaylān, but it is weaker; they do not incline ʿabdan or kaslān because those lack yāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some incline qazḥan and ʿalaman by treating their kasra as though it were yāʾ, and use the same analogy for al-najjādain.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | In genitive forms such as ʿajlānik and mālin kathīr, speakers incline by analogy with bābik and with māshin and dāʿin.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r28] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Speakers differ at pause: some keep imāla, while others open the alif because pausing removes the supporting kasra.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r29] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some incline ʿimādan by analogy with imāla after kasra, while others keep ʿalaman and ʿimādan open without preceding yāʾ or kasra.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A single intervening mobile consonant does not block imāla from an initial kasra, as in ʿimād.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r30] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some pause with bimālin min ʿindi llāh or li-Zaydin māl, analogizing to ʿimād; this is weaker than a connected kasra.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r31] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | They do not say dhā māl this way because a medial alif resembles that of fāʿil; in ʿimādan the second alif follows the first in imāla.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r32] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The second alif in ʿimādan is inclined by the imāla of the first.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In longer nouns from a wāw root, the final alif may incline toward yāʾ once the form has developed a yāʾ, the relevant pattern for musammā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Two intervening consonants still permit imāla when the first is quiescent, since a sākin is a weak barrier.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أهل الحجاز | reports | Hijazis do not apply imāla to the described forms such as sirbāl, shamāl, ʿimād, and kilāb.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | No imāla occurs when the following vowel is fatḥa or ḍamma: fatḥa is closer to alif, while rounding toward wāw would change the letter.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A preceding fatḥa or ḍamma also prevents imāla, as in ribāb, jimād, and al-balbāl.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتمالفيهالألفات)#715/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some incline the alif of as-siwidād because widād behaves like kilāb, a form that accepts imāla.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Hamzat al-waṣl is prefixed so speech can begin before a quiescent consonant; it is an added, vowelled onset.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Sībawayh reports Yunus's account that some speakers say īm Allāh with kasra, then līm Allāh by analogy with the waṣl in ibn.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Waṣl occurs in imperatives of form I when the next consonant is quiescent, in forms such as infaʿala, ifʿalla, and iftaʿala, and in five further derived patterns including istafʿala.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The alif in afʿala is formative rather than an added onset for a quiescent consonant, so its conjugation behaves like a four-letter verb.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A waṣl alif drops after preceding speech because earlier words remove the need for an onset; Sībawayh compares this to dropping hāʾ in vocative speech.

دمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | At the start of speech, waṣl is normally kasra but takes ḍamma when the third letter has ḍamma.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh cites al-Nuʿmān b. Bashīr's line as a poetic example following the rule for adjusting vowels together.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Alif-lām identifies nouns and behaves like qad or sawfa; Ghaylan's line uses bi-dhal and bi-jal, and Sībawayh says the lām is not broken once the form is complete.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil treats the article as separable like qad and sawfa but meaningful; its initial fatḥa distinguishes it, and it remains before an interrogative alif to distinguish question from statement.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايتقدمأولالحروفوهيزائدةقدمتلإسكانأولالحروف)#723/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An unnamed poet's līman Allāh attests the connected onset in the oath expression.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايجريفيهبعضماذكرناإذاكسرللجمععلىالأصل)#785/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Broken plurals on the fiʿāl pattern can yield expanded forms such as diyāwīr and qiyāwīm.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايجريفيهبعضماذكرناإذاكسرللجمععلىالأصل)#785/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ʿAwār forms ʿawāwīr without hamza, unlike the hamza-bearing pattern; its morphology follows a different base form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايجريفيهبعضماذكرناإذاكسرللجمععلىالأصل)#785/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Weak yāʾ and wāw immediately after alif are treated as word-final radicals, like in siqāʾ and qiḍāʾ; an intervening consonant restores the regular form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايجريفيهبعضماذكرناإذاكسرللجمععلىالأصل)#785/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When separation from the word ending preserves the weak radical, forms such as al-shaqāwa and al-ghiwāya retain the underlying wāw or yāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايجريفيهبعضماذكرناإذاكسرللجمععلىالأصل)#785/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The farther weak radicals stand from the word end, the stronger preservation of the base: zawwār and ṣawwām retain wāw, as do akhwa and abwa.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Plural patterns such as masājid and mafātīḥ resist further broken pluralization as endpoint patterns; as male names they take sound masculine plurals and as female names sound feminine plurals.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Plural patterns that already have broken plural forms can be broken again as names: examples include aʿdāl to aʿādīl and aqwāl to aqāwīl, alongside abyāt, anʿām, and ajriba.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A plural-derived name such as aʿbud can take both a diminutive and a broken plural, yielding al-aʿābid, because its pattern permits these processes like a singular.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A three-consonant plural pattern used as a name follows the broken plural expected of a singular with that form, since it can shift into singular-like patterns and diminutives.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A man named on the fuʿūl pattern may form faʿāʾil, since fuʿūl can also be singular and behaves like an existing plural pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A man named Jamāl on a pattern like singular jirāb takes the broken plural expected of a singular of that form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايكسرمماكسرللجمعومالايكسرمنأبنيةالجمعإذاجعلته#590/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Tamra used as a name has shifted from its original meaning and behaves like qaṣʿa, allowing tamār just as qaṣʿa allows qiṣāʿ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A following kasra on ر can make a preceding open vowel incline toward kasra: the ر is like two kasra-bearing consonants, so Sibawayh analogizes its effect to ي.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Imala is blocked when an open vowel follows the alif or when an emphatic consonant resists it, as in المحاذر and حاضر.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With ابن مذعور, the speaker approaches kasra after ر but does not incline the و, since it does not resemble ي and tilting it would also tilt what precedes.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A following separate word with ر and kasra can cause imala across the word boundary, as in خبط رياح and قفا رياح.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Other speakers leave forms uninclined when the conditioning kasra is too far away across a word boundary, as in مال قاسم, خبط رياح, and قفا رياح.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايمالمنالحروفالتيليسبعدهاألفإذاكانتالراءبعدها#721/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some speakers incline before ر in من عمرو but not من الشرق because the latter ر is followed by an emphatic consonant; this also blocks the pattern in مارق.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A doubled verb has two identical consonants at its end, as in رددت and وددت; this is the morphological class of the verse's مضارّ form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | When both final consonants are vowelled, Arabs agree on assimilation; al-Khalil says it is especially apt because repeating the same articulation is burdensome.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أهل الحجاز | reports | The Hijaz dialect keeps the doubled consonants separate when the verb ending is quiescent, moving the preceding consonant to avoid two sukūns together.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بنو تميم | reports | Banu Tamim assimilate the jussive as well as fully vowelled forms; Sibawayh says many other Arabs share this dialect pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If the consonant before the first of the doubled pair is quiescent, it takes that consonant’s vowel; a now-unneeded alif of connection is deleted.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمضاعفالفعلواختلافالعربفيه)#646/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With an alif before the doubled consonants and no alif of connection, the form remains unchanged; لا تضار is one of Sibawayh’s examples.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In ‘إني مما أفعل,’ ما can combine with من as one unit, as in ربما; Abū Ḥayya al-Numayrī’s line illustrates ربما.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nouns such as أهل and مخافة can be annexed directly to an أن-clause, with the sense of أهل لأن يفعل and مخافة لأن يفعل.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some Arabs say ‘لحق أنه ذاهب’ to mean ‘يقين أنه ذاهب,’ but this usage is not common to all Arabs.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | خليق accepts either لأن يفعل or أن يفعل; عسيت أن تفعل similarly follows near-approach verbs such as قاربت and دنوت.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | عسى and اخلولقت take an أن-clause without a verbal-noun alternative here; Arabs do not say ‘عسيت الفعل’ or ‘عسيت للفعل.’
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | عسى is usually invariant across singular, plural, and feminine subjects, though some Arabs inflect it; with inflected forms, أن is accusative as in عسيت أن.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some Arabs use عسى يفعل like كاد يفعل, with a finite verb replacing the accusative noun in the proverb ‘عسى الغوير أبؤسا’; poetry attests this use.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | كاد and كرب normally take a finite verb without أن; poetry permits كاد أن by analogy with عسى, and لعل أن by analogy with عسيت أن.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | يوشك أن تجيء attaches أن to يوشك; توشك أن تجيء is like قاربت أن تفعل, while poetry also uses يوشك يجيء by analogy with عسى.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In ‘أن تضل إحداهما,’ the preposition is omitted; the clause is treated like a verbal noun, as if it said ‘لأن تضل إحداهما.’
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl explains al-Farazdaq’s ‘إن أذنا قتيبة حزتا’ by avoiding separation of أن from its verb, as with كي; it follows إن, which permits nouns before verbs.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After temporal بعد, أن plus a verb stands for a verbal noun; likewise ‘أما أن أسير’ means ‘أما السيرورة.’
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ‘ما منعك أن تأتينا’ means ‘what prevented you from coming to us’: من is omitted before the أن-clause.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأنالتيتكونوالفعلبمنزلةمصدر)#510/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · autho

[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنحتىتنصبعلىوجهينPageV03P016فأحدهماأنتجعلالدخولغاية#471/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Indicative after حتى can describe an entry that immediately follows and is connected with the movement; حتى then introduces a clause like إذا rather than expressing a goal or purpose.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنحتىتنصبعلىوجهينPageV03P016فأحدهماأنتجعلالدخولغاية#471/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Indicative حتى can also introduce a present result after an earlier completed action, as in illness that has now made recovery unlikely; this is not a continuous endpoint.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنحتىتنصبعلىوجهينPageV03P016فأحدهماأنتجعلالدخولغاية#471/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Both indicative constructions are particles of inception with the same basic sense; they differ in whether the later action occurred together with the earlier one or is a present result of it.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنحتىتنصبعلىوجهينPageV03P016فأحدهماأنتجعلالدخولغاية#471/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The Farazdaq's حتى كليب and Ḥassān ibn Thābit's حتى لا تهر support the inceptive use of حتى; the camel example likewise describes a present event after the clause.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنحتىتنصبعلىوجهينPageV03P016فأحدهماأنتجعلالدخولغاية#471/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbada's verse illustrates a connected sequence: the later riding and the earlier departure both belong to the past, and neither occurs without the other.
[SIBAWAYH:شبهوهبمايشبهمنالأسماءبالمصادرنحوقولكفاهms167إلىفىوليسبالفاعل#190/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Al-awwalu fa-l-awwalu resembles source-like nouns without matching them in every respect, functioning like wāḥidan fa-wāḥidan or rajulan rajulan.
[SIBAWAYH:شبهوهبمايشبهمنالأسماءبالمصادرنحوقولكفاهms167إلىفىوليسبالفاعل#190/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In an imperative, accusative al-awwalu fa-l-awwalu is standard; it cannot be a badal or adjective because the corresponding readings are invalid.
[SIBAWAYH:شبهوهبمايشبهمنالأسماءبالمصادرنحوقولكفاهms167إلىفىوليسبالفاعل#190/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · عيسى | reports | ʿĪsā explains the imperative as meaning li-yadkhul, “let the first enter,” and parses the phrase according to that underlying meaning.
[SIBAWAYH:شبهوهبمايشبهمنالأسماءبالمصادرنحوقولكفاهms167إلىفىوليسبالفاعل#190/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Adding wa-l-ṣaghīru wa-l-kabīru permits nominative because the phrase means “all of them.”
[SIBAWAYH:شبهوهبمايشبهمنالأسماءبالمصادرنحوقولكفاهms167إلىفىوليسبالفاعل#190/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When the words are intended as direct adjectives, fa cannot join them; wa is acceptable, as supported by Umayyah ibn Abī ʿĀʾidh's verse.
[SIBAWAYH:شبهوهبمايشبهمنالأسماءبالمصادرنحوقولكفاهms167إلىفىوليسبالفاعل#190/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أمية بن أبي عائذ | reports | Umayyah's poem with wa-shaʿthin supports coordination by wa; substituting fa before shaʿthin would be poor usage.
[SIBAWAYH:شبهوهبمايشبهمنالأسماءبالمصادرنحوقولكفاهms167إلىفىوليسبالفاعل#190/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl allows al-awwalu fa-l-awwalu wa-l-awsaṭu wa-l-ākhiru by treating the sequence as a badal construction like kullukum.
[SIBAWAYH:فالحروفالتيتشركالواووالفاءوثموأووذلكقولكأريدأنتأتينيثم#480/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Mentioning possible error explains the reason for the reminder, as preparing support for a wall explains the cause without intending it to lean.
[SIBAWAYH:فالحروفالتيتشركالواووالفاءوثموأووذلكقولكأريدأنتأتينيثم#480/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أهل الكوفة | reports | The Kufans read فتذكر with indicative mood.
[SIBAWAYH:فالحروفالتيتشركالواووالفاءوثموأووذلكقولكأريدأنتأتينيثم#480/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In 2:282, فتذكر is subjunctive because witnessing is commanded so that one woman may remind the other; error is a cause, not the intended aim.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Tāʾ and dāl share a place and strong articulation; ṭāʾ may assimilate to dāl, but speakers can preserve its emphatic quality because it is audible.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ṭāʾ, tāʾ, and dāl can assimilate into ḍād because its articulation approaches lām and the tooth roots; clarity is easier with its looser articulation.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ḍād resists assimilation into ṣād, sīn, and zāy because its extended articulation acts as a barrier, much as shīn does.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ṭāʾ, dāl, and tāʾ assimilate into shīn due to its extended articulation; the related dental group can also assimilate, though clear pronunciation is good.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Assimilation possible with a quiescent first consonant is also possible when it is moving, as with geminates; adjacent consonants within one word are heavier than those across a boundary.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In derived forms, proximity can prompt substitution or assimilation: ṣabara yields muṣṭabir or muṣbir, while forms such as muzdān and mismiʿ show related adjustments.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Before tāʾ, ẓāʾ can retain emphasis or assimilate after substitution with ṭāʾ; Sībawayh cites Zuhayr's yẓlim / yṭlim rhyme and prefers the regular assimilation direction.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | The regular direction of assimilation has the second consonant follow the first; Sībawayh therefore regards muṭʿan and muṭlam as more analogical than reversed forms.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Dhāl before tāʾ becomes dāl in mudhakkir; the Qur'anic mudakkir exemplifies this, while *mudhdakkir is barred because the letters assimilate reciprocally when separated. | mentions 54:17
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ḍād behaves like ṣād when combined with tāʾ: forms may show partial or complete assimilation, and the common word-internal pattern makes this stronger than across words.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعض العرب | reports | Some Arabs remove ṭāʾ's emphatic quality and make it like dāl when they fully assimilate it; assimilation also proceeds in the reverse direction to ṭāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Some speakers use ṭāʾ in muṭjaʿ; Sībawayh explains its assimilation through the combination of emphaticness, proximity, and frequent co-occurrence within a word.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | With the inflectional suffix tāʾ, the clearest and best Arabic leaves the suffix unchanged; unlike the fixed augment in iftaʿala, it marks a grammatical person and is separable.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعضهم | reports | Some speakers nevertheless assimilate the inflectional tāʾ, saying ʿaddahu for ʿadattahu and naqadahu for naqdattahu by analogy with other forms.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Assimilation normally requires the first consonant to be quiescent; this blocks it in forms such as istaṭʿama, istaḍʿafa, and istadraka.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Hijazis preserve the two consonants in forms such as arدد, while Tamim assimilate them; inflection can move the letters in the latter pattern, unlike the relevant close-consonant forms.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Istādara, istaṭāra, and istaḍāʾa resist assimilation because their sīn is inherently quiescent and the following consonant is already moved; ikhtaṣamū and iqtatalū differ because their radicals are naturally moving.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Watad and waṭad avoid assimilation to prevent confusion with geminated roots and the combined loss of a weak radical; muḥtad likewise stays distinct because tāʾ may correspond to dāl.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The t-prefix assimilates in yatatawwaʿūn, yatadhakkarūn, and yatasammaʿūn; clear forms remain good Arabic because both consonants are moving. | mentions 7:131
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r28] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When initial consonants assimilate, an initial alif is added where needed to avoid starting with a cluster; Sībawayh gives commands such as iṭawwaʿ and idhkur.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r29] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Qur'anic forms support contraction of t-initial forms: fa-ddāraʾtum for fata-dāraʾtum, izzayyanat for tazayyanat, and iṭṭayyarna for taṭayyarna. | mentions 2:72, 10:24, 27:47
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Tāʾ and dāl assimilate to one another because they share a place and differ mainly in voicing; unassimilated speech is possible but laborious.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r30] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When two t-prefixes meet, speakers may retain both or delete the second; Qur'anic examples show both retention and deletion, with the deletable consonant being the one subject to assimilation. | mentions 41:30, 32:16, 97:4, 3:143
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r31] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The present-tense t-prefix is not made quiescent and does not take a linking alif, s

[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r32] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أهل الكوفة | reports | Sībawayh reports a Kūfan reading that contracts tatadhakkarūn to tadhakkarūn; deleting the root dhāl as well would damage the word.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r33] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | rejects | The altered dāl in forms such as mudhakkir is anomalous, resembling a speech error rather than a regular sound change.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The nasal sound of mīm helps speakers articulate adjacent strong consonants distinctly; blocking the nose makes mīm resemble the preceding consonant more closely.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ṣād with sīn or zāy behaves like ṭāʾ with dāl or tāʾ; speakers may preserve or remove emphaticness, with its removal more apt before sīn.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The sibilants and dental stops assimilate across nearby tongue-tip places; Sībawayh cites Ibn Muqbil's verse for tāʾ assimilating into ṣād.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some reciters pronounce lā yasmaʿūn for lā yatسمmaʿūn; Sībawayh treats the clearer form as good Arabic because the articulation places differ. | mentions 37:8
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ẓāʾ, dhāl, and thāʾ form a related dental group and can assimilate among themselves or with nearby ṭāʾ, dāl, and tāʾ; clear articulation is often preferable.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيحروفطرفاللسانوالثنايا#809/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ṣād, sīn, and zāy resist assimilation into the less resonant dental stops because their sibilant sound is more perceptible; rāʾ likewise resists because of its trill.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنماذكرليبينلكوجهنصبهكماذكرمعنىسبحاناللهPageV01P352|#149/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو الخطاب | reports | Abū al-Khaṭṭāb explains ألب على something as persisting with it and أسعد someone as supporting him; لبيك and سعديك accordingly express nearness and following.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنماذكرليبينلكوجهنصبهكماذكرمعنىسبحاناللهPageV01P352|#149/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Addressed to God, لبيك and سعديك mean that the speaker will not distance himself from God's commands and will follow and obey them.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنماذكرليبينلكوجهنصبهكماذكرمعنىسبحاناللهPageV01P352|#149/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | لبيك and سعديك are not ordinary verbal nouns like سقيا and حمدا: their source verbs and same-root verbal nouns are unavailable, so their accusative is explained through a synonymous expression, as سبحان الله is explained by براءة الله.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنماذكرليبينلكوجهنصبهكماذكرمعنىسبحاناللهPageV01P352|#149/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | سبح, لبى, and أفف describe uttering the formulas سبحان الله, لبيك, and أف; like هلل for saying لا إله إلا الله, they are utterance verbs rather than ordinary inflected verbal nouns.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In conditional pairs, an explicit كان makes the intended relation clear; after fa, a nominative predicate is more usual because the answer resumes as a new sentence.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In من لد شولا, شولا is accusative because it means a time; an omitted أن كانت supplies that temporal sense, though some allow genitive by broad usage.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ellipsis is limited to particles and constructions where Arabs use it; one cannot extend a deletion pattern to every particle or verb by analogy.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In the poem فإن جزعا وإن إجمال صبر, إن is a shortened إما meaning either, not conditional إن: the fa and lack of a conditional answer support the parse, as in 47:4. | mentions 47:4
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Dropping ما from إما is poetic only; al-Namr ibn Tawlab’s verse illustrates it, and reading the same form as conditional إن requires a separately omitted verb.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Responses such as هلا خيرا or ألا خيرا use an omitted verb that would be spoken; a nominative is possible when a nominative-governing verb is understood.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In أو فرقا خيرا من حب, the accusative answers a question about an action and implies أفرقك; a nominative would instead present فرق as a topic.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After ولو, an apparent noun normally rests on an omitted كان or يكون, so ولو حمارا is preferred; a nominative is possible but remote because لو selects verbs.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An adjective after ولو must be accusative because it cannot stand in place of a noun; the source contrasts ولو باردا with the acceptable noun ائتنى بتمر.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ادفع الشر ولو إصبعا means even if you push it a finger’s breadth or it were a finger; accusative follows the implied action, while raising is less natural.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After news of an arrival or dream, خير مقدم and خيرا can be accusative as an omitted verbal response; nominative makes an independent statement such as هذا خير مقدم.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Accusative after the conditional particle is also possible: the answer is jussive, and its noun is analogized to a predicate, although the analogy is not complete.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Formulae like مصاحب معان and مبرور مأجور are nominative with an understood أنت; راشدا مهديا is commonly accusative with اذهب, though raising is also possible.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A reply صادقا والله after a report means قاله صادقا; its accusative is licensed by the implied act of saying or reciting.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In متعرضا لعنن لم يعنه, the omitted verb is recoverable from the visible situation: the person has approached an undertaking without being summoned to it.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In bargaining, بيع الملطى omits أبايعك; مواعيد عرقوب similarly omits واعدتني because the shared situation and prior history supply the verb.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some Arabs use nominatives such as متعرض or صادق والله; Sibawayh also explains غضب الخيل على اللجم through an implied verb, with some speakers raising it instead.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After someone mentions a person, أهل ذاك or أهله can mean you mentioned his family; accusative follows the semantic act, while nominative supplies هو.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | When the verb is omitted, suppressing the accusative-governing verb is better; omitting a nominative-governing verb also requires omitting its predicate, and extra ellipsis weakens the parse.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A following adjective or appositive tied to the previously mentioned person must be accusative; حق or كذب can instead introduce an independent condition with its own omitted كان or وقع.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yunus reports Hudba ibn Khashram’s verse as an Arabic example of an إن clause whose verbal material is understood from context.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Layla al-Akhyaliyya, Ibn Hammam al-Sululi, and al-Nabigha illustrate accusative adjectives or descriptions that remain tied to the person named earlier in the clause.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yunus attributes to some Arabs إن لا صالح فطالح, understood as an omitted مررت clause: if I did not meet a righteous person, I met a wicked one.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | rejects | Sibawayh calls that analysis weak because it requires an extra omitted verb after إن لا; the fuller إن لا يكن صالحا فطالح requires less ellipsis.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكالناسمجزيونبأعمالهمإنخيرافخيروإنشرافشروالمرء#103/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | إن of condition does not directly govern a noun: any accusative or nominative after it depends on an omitted verb, while a genitive name belongs to a suppressed prepositional phrase such as مررت بزيد.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكماأحسنعبدالله|زعمالخليلأنهبمنزلةقولكشئأحسنعبد#44/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil explains mā aḥsana ʿAbd Allāh as an exclamation, conceptually like saying shayʾu
