n aḥsana ʿAbd Allāh; that paraphrase is illustrative, not an utterance.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكماأحسنعبدالله|زعمالخليلأنهبمنزلةقولكشئأحسنعبد#44/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The exclamative construction has fixed order and cannot be recast as mā yaḥsunu or another ordinary verb form; it uses one pattern because speakers do not conjugate it.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكماأحسنعبدالله|زعمالخليلأنهبمنزلةقولكشئأحسنعبد#44/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The form can derive from roots such as ḥasuna, karuma, and aʿṭā yet behaves as a fixed nominal pattern, like lāta and mā; ajdal is likewise treated as a noun despite its verbal root.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكماأحسنعبدالله|زعمالخليلأنهبمنزلةقولكشئأحسنعبد#44/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In innī mimmā an aṣnaʿ, mā alone is a noun meaning the matter.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكماأحسنعبدالله|زعمالخليلأنهبمنزلةقولكشئأحسنعبد#44/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Naʿman in ghusiltuhu ghaslan naʿman means excellent washing, literally niʿma al-ghusl.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكماأحسنعبدالله|زعمالخليلأنهبمنزلةقولكشئأحسنعبد#44/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Adding kāna in mā kāna aḥsana Zaydan marks the exclamation as referring to the past.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبكلقائماومررتببعضقائماوببعضجالسا|وإنما#251/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With an omitted complement, kull and baʿḍ are neither modifiers nor modified nouns; treating them as adjectives is awkward because it departs from their normal annexation.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبكلقائماومررتببعضقائماوببعضجالسا|وإنما#251/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Deleting the complement leaves kull and baʿḍ definite by association with a definite noun; Sībawayh compares this unusual ellipsis with other Arabic omissions.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبكلقائماومررتببعضقائماوببعضجالسا|وإنما#251/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Kull and baʿḍ are not adjectives; they occur sentence-initially or are built on a preceding noun or other element, as in the cited Qur'anic example. | mentions 27:87
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبكلقائماومررتببعضقائماوببعضجالسا|وإنما#251/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Jamiʿ can function like rajul in this construction; the Qur'anic example and Arabs' usage show it as a predicate meaning assembled. | mentions 36:32
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبكلقائماومررتببعضقائماوببعضجالسا|وإنما#251/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | prefers | Khalil regards predicative kulluhum as weak and prefers it as a subject or modifier after its antecedent; Sībawayh says Arab usage confirmed his account.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبكلقائماومررتببعضقائماوببعضجالسا|وإنما#251/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Khalil accepts أكلت شاة كل شاة but considers أكلت كل شاة weak, since kull does not normally generalize without an antecedent.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبكلقائماومررتببعضقائماوببعضجالسا|وإنما#251/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Kulluhum resembles emphatic forms such as ajmaʿīn and anfusahum, which modify rather than serve as predicates; it can nevertheless be predicative, albeit weakly.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبكلقائماومررتببعضقائماوببعضجالسا|وإنما#251/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Kulluhum, both dual forms, and kulluhunna follow the same pattern; jamiʿhum can also be an adjective or a noun-like subject or predicate.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبكلقائماومررتببعضقائماوببعضجالسا|وإنما#251/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Kull shayʾ and kull rajul must be annexed to another element because they cannot be used adjectivally.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبهمجمعياوعامةوجماعةكأنكقلتمررتبهمقياما|#173/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl treats expressions such as جميعا and عامة as circumstantial accusatives; these are inflected nouns, unlike adjectives, and circumstantial expressions normally stay indefinite and unannexed.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبهمجمعياوعامةوجماعةكأنكقلتمررتبهمقياما|#173/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | rejects | Yūnus analyzes وحده like عنده and groups خمستهم, الجماء الغفير, قضهم, طرا, and قاطبة with circumstantial expressions; Sībawayh rejects this comparison because وحده and فاه إلى فيه do not have the same referent structure.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبهمجمعياوعامةوجماعةكأنكقلتمررتبهمقياما|#173/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | prefers | Al-Khalīl treats وحده as an accusative circumstantial meaning خصوصا, equivalent to مررت به واحده; Sībawayh adopts this first analysis over Yūnus's.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبهمجمعياوعامةوجماعةكأنكقلتمررتبهمقياما|#173/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | كلهم, جميعهم, أجمعون, عامتهم, and أنفسهم function only as adjectives, never as circumstantial expressions.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبهمجمعياوعامةوجماعةكأنكقلتمررتبهمقياما|#173/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | طرا and قاطبة can naturally be indefinite circumstantial nouns even when they are not verbal nouns, which makes them closer to Yūnus's comparison than وحده is.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاأولفارسمقبلوهذاكلمتاععندكموضوعوهذاخيرمنك#249/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أول, كل, and خير can be indefinite when attached to an indefinite and can describe one; the following noun behaves as an indefinite adjective.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاأولفارسمقبلوهذاكلمتاععندكموضوعوهذاخيرمنك#249/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A definite description identifies or distinguishes someone already known and therefore cannot normally be used as an indefinite-style circumstantial phrase without confusing it with an indefinite noun.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاأولفارسمقبلوهذاكلمتاععندكموضوعوهذاخيرمنك#249/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl reports the Shammākh's verse using كل as an adjective of an indefinite خليل, supporting its indefinite use.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاأولفارسمقبلوهذاكلمتاععندكموضوعوهذاخيرمنك#249/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو الخطاب | reports | Abū al-Khaṭṭāb reports a verse heard from reliable Arab speakers in which كل describes the indefinite فتى.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاأولفارسمقبلوهذاكلمتاععندكموضوعوهذاخيرمنك#249/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | rejects | The accusative in أول فارس مقبلا does not make أول definite; the phrase means one of the horsemen, with من الفرسان omitted for brevity.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاأولفارسمقبلوهذاكلمتاععندكموضوعوهذاخيرمنك#249/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The omitted phrase is من الفرسان; it is not evidence that a numeral complement such as درهما in عشرون درهما is definite.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاأولفارسمقبلوهذاكلمتاععندكموضوعوهذاخيرمنك#249/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · عيسى | reports | ʿĪsā allows مقبلا in the accusative as a circumstantial predicate, and al-Khalīl also accepts this analysis; the nominative remains the preferred form.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاأولفارسمقبلوهذاكلمتاععندكموضوعوهذاخيرمنك#249/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus reports Arabs saying مررت بماء قعدة رجل and identifies the genitive as the proper case in this construction.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاأولفارسمقبلوهذاكلمتاععندكموضوعوهذاخيرمنك#249/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A descriptive adjective of an indefinite normally stays indefinite; an accusative circumstantial use is marked when the expression describes the first noun itself, though it can be a separate state.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاأولفارسمقبلوهذاكلمتاععندكموضوعوهذاخيرمنك#249/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · رؤبة | reports | Ruʾba uses غلام لك مقبلا as a circumstantial phrase separate from the first noun, showing that an indefinite noun may take a circumstantial description.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In coordinated clauses, the nearer verb governs the noun visibly, while the first predication remains understood; the listener recovers it without giving one noun both nominative and accusative roles.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If the following noun is the nearer verb's subject, an earlier verb still needs an understood subject; a verb may lack an object but cannot lack a subject.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | In ḍarabnī wa-ḍarabtuhum qawmuka, the noun can be raised by the nearer verb with an understood pronoun; apposition instead requires the plural ḍarabūnī.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A nominative noun after ḍarabtu wa-ḍarabnī is usual; accusative Zaydan is possible by analogy with expressions such as matā raʾayta Zaydan munṭaliqan.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ḍarabnī wa-ḍarabtu qawmuka is possible but awkward if treated as singular; special agreement such as huwa aḥsan al-fityān wa-ajmaluhu does not generalize to ordinary noun phrases.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash calls the singular-agreement analysis poor by analogy and warns it could wrongly license forms such as aṣḥābuka jalasa.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Al-Farazdaq, Ṭufayl al-Ghanawī, and a poet of Bāhila illustrate clauses where the first verb is understood semantically while the second governs in form and meaning; their lines include سبني, جرى, and تصبى.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ʿUmar b. Abī Rabīʿa illustrates an understood subject pronoun appearing in the latter clause of the coordinated construction.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Al-Marrār al-Asadī's verse supplies another poetic example of the coordinated construction and its understood pronoun.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Imruʾ al-Qays uses قليل as nominative because little money is not what he seeks; making it the object

 of طلب would distort the intended meaning.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh cites Qur'an 33:35 as evidence that a later coordinated form can leave unexpressed material already supplied by the earlier form. | mentions 33:35
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The nearer governor is preferred for proximity and because the listener can recover the earlier predication; prepositional phrases show the same attachment principle.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Qays b. al-Khaṭīm's coordinated نحن and أنت share the predicate rāḍ, illustrating understood material across clauses.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ḍābiʾ al-Burjumī coordinates the speaker with Qiyār under a shared predicate, another poetic case of understood material.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Ibn Aḥmar uses a singular predicate for himself and his father; the listener understands that the quality applies to both.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Al-Farazdaq omits a predicate after the first coordinated clause because the later predicate lets the listener recover it.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | The preferred construction uses the nearer verb without putting a singular form for a plural, or a plural for a singular; poetry further illustrates the rule.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكضربتوضربنىزيدوضربنىوضربتزيداتحملالاسمعلىالفعلالذى#46/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With a first singular verb followed by a plural verb and a noun, the form is licensed either by the akalūnī al-barāghīth dialect or by apposition to the plural pronoun.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكفيرجلاسمهراديارادأقبلوإنماكانتالكسرةأولىالحركات#343/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When a man named Rād is addressed as yā Rād, kasra is restored because that is the vowel the consonant would have had without assimilation.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكفيرجلاسمهراديارادأقبلوإنماكانتالكسرةأولىالحركات#343/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In truncating Mufarr, the first rāʾ remains quiescent because its preceding consonant is vowelled.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكفيرجلاسمهراديارادأقبلوإنماكانتالكسرةأولىالحركات#343/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Truncated Muḥmār and Muḍārr retain the vowel of the original doubled form; the passive-intended Muḍārr is likewise treated as shortened from muḍārrar.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكفيرجلاسمهراديارادأقبلوإنماكانتالكسرةأولىالحركات#343/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The first rāʾ of a doubled form is not an ordinary augment and should not be deleted with the second; its behavior differs from genuine augment letters.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكفيرجلاسمهراديارادأقبلوإنماكانتالكسرةأولىالحركات#343/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When Asḥār loses its final rāʾ, the preceding quiescent rāʾ must be vowelled to avoid two adjacent quiescent consonants.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكفيرجلاسمهراديارادأقبلوإنماكانتالكسرةأولىالحركات#343/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The fatḥa on Asḥār's rāʾ follows the nearest vowel source, like the vowel placed on the last consonant in jussive geminates.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكفيرجلاسمهراديارادأقبلوإنماكانتالكسرةأولىالحركات#343/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · رجل من أزد السراة | reports | A man of Azd al-Sarāt is cited reciting a line about a child and father, supporting the rule that the nearest vowel supplies the movement.
[SIBAWAYH:وهوقولكفيرجلاسمهراديارادأقبلوإنماكانتالكسرةأولىالحركات#343/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Asḥār differs from Muḥmār: Muḥmār's underlying form has two rāʾs, while Asḥār is inherently assimilated and its first rāʾ is only quiescent.
[FARRA:v1p185/r1] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | In إلا أن تكون تجارة حاضرة تديرونها, تديرونها may be accusative or nominative; an indefinite noun can take a verbal predicate in either position.
[FARRA:v1p185/r2] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | A definite noun cannot be replaced by its verb as predicate in the same way, because a definite noun is specified while an indefinite one is open-ended.
[FARRA:v1p185/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · المفضل الضبي | reports | Al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī recited poetry with الحميم الحميم, where the second repeats and intensifies the first; without it, the first would be nominative.
[FARRA:v1p185/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | In وإن كان ذو عسرة, nominative ذو is possible; ʿAbd Allāh and Ubayy instead read accusative ذا, implying an omitted subject of كان.
[FARRA:v1p185/r5] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The accusative with كان requires an understood, indefinite subject; the cited poetry supplies such a subject and illustrates the construction.
[FARRA:v1p185/r6] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | When the noun is overt, as in فإن كن نساء, the predicate can still be nominative or accusative, as in the cited trade construction.
[FARRA:v1p187/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | ولا يضار الكاتب والشاهد means do not summon either while occupied.
[MAJAZ:v1p82/r9] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Lā yabkhas means not to diminish; the proverb describes her as foolish but unjust.
[MAJAZ:v1p83/r1] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | أن تضل إحداهما means that one of the two forgets.
[MAJAZ:v1p83/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | A witness who has already testified must not refuse a summons; before witnessing, the person may choose not to testify.
[MAJAZ:v1p83/r3] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | أقسط means more just.
[MAJAZ:v1p83/r4] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | فسوق means sin in this context.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p110#2/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says a witness must not refuse when called to give testimony.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p110#2/r2] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says the prohibition covers both withholding testimony one already has and refusing to testify when summoned.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p110#2/r3] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid interprets the summons as applying to witnesses who have already testified.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p110#2/r4] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid, as reported by Jabir al-Ju‘fi, says a witness may choose whether to testify until he has testified.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p110#2/r5] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · عطاء ومجاهد | reports | Ata and Mujahid say the scribe is obliged to write, while the witness clause concerns someone who has already witnessed the matter.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p110#2/r6] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says a scribe is harmed by being made to write what was not dictated, and a witness by being made to attest what he did not witness.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p110#2/r7] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · عطاء | reports | Ata says the scribe and witness must deliver what is entrusted to them.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p110#2/r8] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · عمر | reports | Ikrima reports Umar reciting the verb with a doubled r, as ‘ولا يضارر كاتب ولا شهيد.’
[AKHFASH:v1p205/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | فرجل وامرأتان means the witnesses to be summoned are one man and two women.
[AKHFASH:v1p205/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | تسأم is from the verb سئمت, with the listed verbal nouns سآمة, سأمة, سآما, and سأما.
[AKHFASH:v1p205/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | يأب is jussive because it is a prohibition; at pause it is pronounced without a final yāʾ.
[AKHFASH:v1p205/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | تكون in إلا أن تكون تجارة حاضرة can mean 'occur'; alternatively it can take an accusative predicate with an implied subject, تلك.
[AKHFASH:v1p205/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | ولا يضار can be parsed as a prohibition or as an indicative statement; compare لا تضار والدة بولدها, though that form was not read in the indicative. | mentions 2:233
[AKHFASH:v1p205/r6] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | بدين reinforces تداينتم, since mutual lending already conveys debt, like سجَدَ الملائكة كلهم أجمعون. | mentions 15:30
[AKHFASH:v1p205/r7] AKHFASH, d. 215 · الشاعر | reports | A rajaz line using داينت illustrates reciprocal dealing: داينتُها وداينتني yields تداينا.
[AKHFASH:v1p205/r8] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | In أن تكتبوه صغيرا أو كبيرا, الشاهد is understood; إلى أجله refers to the deadline through which the testimony is valid.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p5/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · الآخر | rejects | An unnamed interpreter says each woman is made equivalent to a male, so the two together stand for one man and one reminds the other.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p99#2/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | وليّه means the guardian of the party whose right is owed.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p99#2/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | أن تضل means that one woman forgets the testimony and the other reminds her; Moses' phrase uses ضالّ for forgetful. | mentions 26:20
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p99#2/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | ولا تسأموا means do not grow tired.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p99#2/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | The written record should include the debt whether it is small or large.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p99#2/r5] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | أقسط means more just; the record strengthens testimony because it reminds witnesses of all they witnessed.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p99#2/r6] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | أدنى ألا ترتابوا means less likely to doubt.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p99#2/r7] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | A present trade means goods the parties buy and sell among themselves.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p99#2/r8] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | The writer must not be made to record what was not dictated, nor the witness to testify without being summoned; another view says they

may refuse a summons.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p99#2/r9] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · مجاهد والكلبي | reports | Mujāhid and al-Kalbī explain لا يضار as not bothering a writer by distracting him from his trade or work.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p221/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · أكثر العلماء | reports | Most scholars treat the relevant ruling in Surat al-Ma'ida as decisive and unrepealed because that sura was the last revealed.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p221/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · بعضهم | reports | Some hold that the relevant ruling in al-Ma'ida was abrogated by the testimony rule of two men or one man and two women.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p254/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Ḍalāl can mean forgetting: the forgetful person turns away from a matter and its recollection.
[TAB-FULL:v1p55/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · زيد بن ثابت | reports | Zayd reports that after Yamāma's losses, ʿUmar urged collecting the Qur'an; Abū Bakr initially refused because the Prophet had not done so, then accepted the proposal and assigned Zayd.
[TAB-FULL:v1p55/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · زيد بن ثابت | reports | Zayd says he gathered the Qur'an from parchment, shoulder blades, and palm stalks; the single sheet later passed from Abū Bakr to ʿUmar and Ḥafṣa.
[TAB-FULL:v1p55/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · حذيفة بن اليمان | reports | Ḥudhayfa warned ʿUthmān after seeing Syrians and Iraqis recite differently in Armenia and accuse each other's readings of unbelief.
[TAB-FULL:v1p55/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عثمان بن عفان | reports | ʿUthmān commissioned Zayd and the eloquent Abān ibn Saʿīd to produce a codex, write what they agreed on, and refer disagreements to him.
[TAB-FULL:v1p55/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عثمان بن عفان | reports | ʿUthmān borrowed Ḥafṣa's sheet, collated the codex without finding differences, returned it, ordered copies made, then after her death reclaimed and erased the sheet.
[TAB-FULL:v1p60/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī argues the community could transmit some of the seven modes and omit the rest; they fulfilled their duty, and preserving every mode could have harmed Islam and its people.
[TAB-FULL:v1p60/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Differences of case ending, vowel, consonant movement, or letter form with the same written outline are unrelated to the seven-aḥruf report, since disputing such variants is not disbelief.
[TAB-FULL:v1p60/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | There is no need to identify the six other dialects: even if known, they are no longer recited today.
[TAB-FULL:v1p60/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | rejects | A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās assigns five modes to the ʿajuz of Hawāzin and two to Quraysh and Khuzāʿa, but al-Ṭabarī rejects its chains as proof: al-Kalbī/Abū Ṣāliḥ and Qatāda, who never met Ibn ʿAbbās.
[TAB-FULL:v5p100/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عطاء | reports | ʿAṭāʾ says those summoned are people who already testified; an initial invitation may be declined because witnesses are plentiful, unlike the scribe's binding duty to write.
[TAB-FULL:v5p100/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says a witness who has testified must answer a summons to deliver and perform that testimony.
[TAB-FULL:v5p100/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says al-Ḥasan interpreted the verse as requiring a person who already has testimony to perform it when summoned.
[TAB-FULL:v5p100/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk includes witnesses who were formally engaged and scribes who wrote a record: when called to adjudicate a right, they must answer and report what they were entrusted with.
[TAB-FULL:v5p100/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عطية العوفي | reports | ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī treats the rule as a recommendation for a man or woman invited to give new testimony, not as an obligation.
[TAB-FULL:v5p100/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عطاء | reports | ʿAṭāʾ is also reported to say that an invitation to give new testimony is a recommendation that may be accepted or declined.
[TAB-FULL:v5p100/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī prefers that the verse obligates an already appointed witness to perform testimony before an authority or judge who can secure the right owed.
[TAB-FULL:v5p101/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī reasons that “the witnesses” names identifiable people already entrusted with testimony, as established by the earlier command to appoint them; it cannot mean everyone merely capable of witnessing.
[TAB-FULL:v5p101/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī says an initial request to witness is obligatory only when no other suitable witness is available, by broader duties to preserve a fellow Muslim's right, not by this verse itself.
[TAB-FULL:v5p103/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Do not grow weary of recording a small or large debt until its term; a written record keeps track of both the due date and amount.
[TAB-FULL:v5p103/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid says the object to be written is the debt.
[TAB-FULL:v5p103/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The verb تسأموا means “do not tire”; Labīd and Zuhayr use سئمت in the sense of becoming weary.
[TAB-FULL:v5p103/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | A Basran grammarian construes “to its term” as the term for the witness, meaning the time during which testimony is valid.
[TAB-FULL:v5p104#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Written documentation makes testimony more accurate because it preserves the parties' exact acknowledged words, keeps witnesses' accounts aligned, and makes judgment clearer; obeying God's command is itself more just than abandoning it.
[TAB-FULL:v5p104/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | “That” means recording the debt through its due date; أَقْسَط means more just and comes from the verb for judging equitably, unlike قَسَط, which means to act unjustly. | mentions 72:15
[TAB-FULL:v5p104/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī glosses أَقْسَط as “more just in God's sight.”
[TAB-FULL:v5p105#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The exception permits leaving a written record for immediate cash trade because each party receives what is due before parting; it does not cover deferred or credit transactions.
[TAB-FULL:v5p105#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī describes the exempt trade as local, visible goods exchanged directly, for which the parties need not write a record.
[TAB-FULL:v5p105#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says debts due at a term must be documented, while immediate hand-to-hand trades should be witnessed though writing is waived.
[TAB-FULL:v5p105#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Most Hijaz, Iraqi, and other reciters raise تجارة حاضرة; some Kufans use the accusative, which is grammatically possible, but al-Ṭabarī prefers the widespread nominative reading.
[TAB-FULL:v5p105/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | أدنى means nearer, and the writing brings the parties closer to certainty rather than doubt about the testimony.
[TAB-FULL:v5p105/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī explains the phrase as ensuring that people will not doubt the testimony.
[TAB-FULL:v5p105/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Writing every debt, large or small, makes the transaction more just, gives witnesses a sounder basis, and helps prevent doubt about the amount and due date.
[TAB-FULL:v5p108/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic permits an indefinite noun with its adjective after kāna to appear either nominative or accusative; poets attest both constructions, so a feminine noun does not require kāna to be feminine.
[TAB-FULL:v5p108/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | Two anonymous poetic examples attest the Arabic construction of an indefinite feminine noun with kāna in these case patterns.
[TAB-FULL:v5p108/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض الناس | reports | Some assume the accusative reading requires the masculine form يكون, as though its sense were “unless it be a trade.”
[TAB-FULL:v5p108/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض نحويي البصرة | reports | Some Basran grammarians treat kāna here as a complete verb meaning “exist” or “occur,” with تجارة حاضرة as its subject and no predicate.
[TAB-FULL:v5p108/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī says the complete-verb analysis is grammatically possible but less apt; تديرونها بينكم can be the predicate in the accusative or follow the indefinite تجارة حاضرة in the nominative.
[TAB-FULL:v5p109/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Even when cash trades need not be written, both parties should have witnesses for every sale, large or small, immediate or deferred, to prevent either buyer or seller from losing a right through denial and lack of proof.

item.text: The early notes show recurring disputes over whether writing is binding, who dictates for an incapable debtor, when a witness must answer a summons, and who is protected by “do not harm.” I’m tracking those separately from the verse’s readings and grammar.

[BAQILLANI:v1p120/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | An accomplished critic recognizes each speaker’s style and ranks speech accurately, including whether a writer excels in only certain genres or throughout.
[BAQILLANI:v1p120/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Poets may excel selectively in praise, invective, humor, or description; an expert knows each person’s limits and can identify their later work.
[BAQILLANI:v1p120/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Style recognition extends across poems, handwriting, letters, and sermons; confusion occurs when two writers briefly adopt similar methods.
[BAQILLANI:v1p120/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Experts distinguish Abu Tammam from al-Buhturi except where the former drops artifice and adopts an easy, bookish style resembling the latter.
[BAQILLANI:v1p120/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The distinct poetic textures of Abu Nuwas and Muslim, and Ibn al-Rumi and al-Buhturi, remain recognizable despite occasional overlap.
[BAQILLANI:v1p120/r6] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | He lists recognizable styles among al-Aʿsha, Imruʾ al-Qays, al-Nabigha, Zuhayr, Jarir, al-Akhtal, al-Baʿith, and al-Farazdaq.
[BAQILLANI:v1p120/r7] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The style of Abd al-Hamid’s generation differs from later letter writers; Ibn al-Amid blended earlier and later methods and developed a recognizable personal manner, despite slight occasional ambiguity.
[BAQILLANI:v1p135/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | reports | The Hudaybiyya treaty set a ten-year truce, returned Quraysh escapees who lacked a guardian’s permission, left Muslim defectors with Quraysh, allowed either side to join either pact, and set the Prophet’s delayed three-day Meccan visit and travel arms.
[BAQILLANI:v1p135/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Baqillani asks literate readers to compare Qur’anic eloquence with the Prophet’s recorded sermons and letters, which he says differ by a wide gulf.
[BAQILLANI:v1p135/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The Qur’an is not simply crafted prophetic rhetoric: sermons at major occasions and letters to kings receive serious effort, yet remain distinct from the Qur’an, which is divine in origin.
[BAQILLANI:v1p135/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Companions’ and other eloquent speakers’ sermons share the Prophet’s human style; their differences are bounded variations among eloquent people, unlike the Qur’an’s distinction.
[BAQILLANI:v1p256/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra says Arabs call one poetic line or a single pearl yatiim, two or three lines a nutfa, up to ten a qitʿa, and twenty a qasida.
[BAQILLANI:v1p256/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The report derives qasida from accumulated marrow, as opposed to scattered marrow, and cites Labid’s stacked ostrich eggs as evidence for the sense of layered accumulation.
[BAQILLANI:v1p256/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | A rare, strange line, familiar proverb, or unusual meaning can occur spontaneously, even without deliberate effort to produce it.
[BAQILLANI:v1p256/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · بعض علماء هذه الصنعة | reports | An unnamed master attributes such exceptional lines to deep command of the craft and broad knowledge, which can yield effects beyond calculation or classification.
[BAQILLANI:v1p256/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | He reaffirms that speech equal in measure to a surah is miraculous.
[BAQILLANI:v1p284/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Punning can be learned from books such as Kitab al-Ajnas and Kitab al-ʿAyn, and antithesis is easier; the eloquence at issue in Qur’anic inimitability cannot be acquired by study.
[BAQILLANI:v1p284/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Learnable capacities converge at a customary limit, like human strength; exceeding that limit breaks convention and can serve as a prophetic sign under the proper conditions.
[BAQILLANI:v1p284/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Exceptional lines or phrases may occur rarely in a poet’s or writer’s work, so a person may be famed for only one or two; if all speech sustained that level, it could be called miraculous.
[BAQILLANI:v1p284/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Humans can produce a fine word or phrase, but cannot compose a surah or equivalent or attain the Qur’an’s level of eloquence and oratory.
[BAQILLANI:v1p284/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | A poetic form may happen to appear in the Qur’an without giving the Qur’an the status of poetry.
[BAQILLANI:v1p284/r6] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · ناس | reports | Some hold that the miraculous measure is an entire surah or the longest verse.

[BAQILLANI:v1p284/r8] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Eloquence means conveying the self’s intended meaning with the best sense and strongest wording, reaching the utterance’s full purpose.
[BAQILLANI:v1p286/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Speech becomes miraculous when it surpasses eloquence’s customary limit and reaches a level even the most accomplished practitioners cannot attain.
[BAQILLANI:v1p286/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The Qur’an differs from other speech in its genre and style and in exceeding the human limit of eloquence.

[BAQILLANI:v1p286/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | After a long challenge and repeated rebukes, the Qur’an alone holds the lead; everyone failed, some recognizing their incapacity without understanding its cause.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p489/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الضحاك والسدي | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddī interpret safīh as a young child.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p489/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · السدي وابن زيد | reports | Al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd explain weak as incapable or mentally deficient.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p489/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Someone unable to dictate may be mute, impaired, or ignorant of what he owns and owes.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p489/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الضحاك وابن زيد | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd say the wali is the guardian of a child, incapable person, or fool: a trustee, heir, or other person acting for him.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p489/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس والربيع ومقاتل | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Rabīʿ, and Muqātil instead say the wali is the creditor, who knows the debt best.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p489/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الزجاج وصاحب النظم | prefers | Al-Zajjāj and the author of al-Naẓm prefer the guardian interpretation: 4:5 calls for guardians to manage dependents’ assets, and taking the creditor as wali would let a claimant’s assertion replace writing and witnesses. | mentions 4:5
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p489/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | The passage’s syntax confirms the dependent’s guardian: the debtor is the one who dictates, so his wali must be his representative; a creditor’s representative would have been framed like the earlier scribe.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p491/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Istashhidū means ashhidū, to call someone as witness; the saying that people testify but are not istushhidūn is explained as saying that they do not testify.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p491/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The two men are free, adult members of the believers’ community, excluding children and enslaved people.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p491/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الزجاج والفراء وصاحب النظم | reports | The phrase one man and two women can mean the witnesses sought should be one man and two women, let there be that combination, or let that number suffice; each syntactic paraphrase is sound.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p491/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الحسن الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash supplies an implicit kāna; it may take a predicate or be complete, with the complete verb preferred because it requires fewer omitted words, though either reading implies testimony by one man and two women.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p491/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | There is consensus that women’s testimony is admissible in matters of property.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p493/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās glosses those whom you approve as people of virtue and religion, like the just witnesses in 65:2; this implies some witnesses should not be accepted. | mentions 65:2
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p493/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The source lists ten qualities for an admissible witness: freedom, adulthood, Islam, uprightness, knowledge, no self-serving interest or self-protective motive, no frequent error, no breach of propriety, and no enmity with the party testified against.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p493/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The purpose clause an taḍilla attaches to an implied command to seek one man and two women; it may attach to an implicit verb or to a supplied predicate.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p495/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس وجميع أهل التفسير والمعاني | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās and exegetes and language scholars take taḍilla as forget, since the forgetful turns away from recall; 26:20 and al-Farazdaq’s verse illustrate it, while Abū ʿAmr says the root means disappearance. | mentions 26:20
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p495/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو علي | reports | Abū ʿAlī says iḥdā is a feminine form of wāḥid that is used only in an annexed phrase, not by itself.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p495/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو العباس عن ابن الأعرابي | reports | Abū al-ʿAbbās transmits Ibn al-Aʿrābī’s forms for pluralizing iḥdā as iḥd, with analogies to kubr/kubrā and poetic attestation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p495/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | An is accusative with a purpose sense: call two women as witnesses so that one can remind the other.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p495/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · سيبويه والبصريون | reports | Sibawayh and the Basran grammarians explain that the verse names forgetting because it causes the needed reminder, as preparing a support because a wall may lean.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p499/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | rejects | Because the clause also says fatudhakkira, the interpretation of an taḍilla as the stated purpose fails: fear of forgetting makes sense, but fear of reminding does not.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p499/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza reads in taḍilla with kasra and fatudhakkira in the indicative; inna is conditional, taḍilla is jussive with a joining fatḥa, and the fāʾ introduces the apodosis.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p499/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · سيبويه | reports | By analogy with 5:95, Sibawayh posits a deleted subject after the apodosis fāʾ, meaning in the matter that one woman reminds the other; the condition and answer modify the indefinite two women. | mentions 5:95
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p499/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | A conditional clause can describe an indefinite noun, as in 22:41; here condition and answer qualify the two women. | mentions 22:41
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p500/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Fatudhakkira is read with either gemination or a light consonant; gemination makes dhakara transitive to a second object, supported by 51:55, 88:21 and a poem, while the light form uses hamza-transitivity and omits the object, meaning the testimony. | mentions 51:55, 88:21
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p500/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · عامة المفسرين | reports | Most exegetes understand the other woman to remind her after she forgets.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p500/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · سفيان بن عيينة | reports | Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna instead interprets it as making the other woman a male witness, so their joint testimony counts as a man’s; this is also attributed to Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ and reported through a narration.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p500/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abū ʿAmr distinguishes the readings: geminated means reminding after forgetting; light means one woman reminds the other because the two together stand in a man’s place.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p500/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المفسرون | rejects | Exegetes reject the male-equivalence interpretation: women without a man still cannot testify, forgetting should be paired with its opposite, remembering, and equal male status would apply across all legal rulings.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p502/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · قتادة والربيع | reports | Qatāda and al-Rabīʿ say the ban on refusing applies when asked to undertake testimony; al-Shaʿbī makes it obligatory only if no one else can do so.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p502/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس عن عطاء | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAṭāʾ, applies it to giving testimony: after entrusting someone with testimony, one may need him to attend court and deliver it.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p502/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مجاهد وعكرمة والسدي وسعيد بن جبير | reports | Mujāhid, ʿIkrima, al-Suddī, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr also understand the verse as testimony’s performance and delivery.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p502/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الحسن وأبو إسحاق | prefers | Al-Ḥasan says the duty covers both undertaking and delivering testimony when the person is available and has no excuse; Abū Isḥāq chooses this view, supported by the adjacent command not to tire of documenting what one witnessed.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p502/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Saʾāma means weariness or annoyance; the infinitive clause is accusative as the object of that weariness, and the pronouns in write it and its due date refer to the debt.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p502/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | prefers | The command not to tire of writing is best addressed to creditors: document the rights they lend, small or large, with due date and term; the passage begins by addressing asset and debt holders, while trivial amounts are not normally recorded.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p504/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Dhālikum refers to the documentation; it is more equitable with God because following God’s command is more just than neglecting it.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p504/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Written records make testimony more reliable because they remind witnesses, instead of leaving them to impressions; aqwam means more fully upright, and adnā means closer to removing doubt about amount and term.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p504/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | A current sale that the parties transact hand to hand can omit documentation because the risks of deferred payment and term are absent.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p504/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Here kāna means occur or come into

 being, as in the usage discussed at 2:280. | mentions 2:280
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p504/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ allows tadīrūnahā to be accusative as the predicate of kāna; otherwise it is nominative describing a present transaction in circulation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p504/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · عاصم | reports | ʿĀṣim reads tijāratan ḥāḍiratan in the accusative; Abū Isḥāq understands an implied present debt transaction.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p504/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو علي | rejects | Abū ʿAlī rejects treating tadāyun or the debt in a person’s liability as the name of kāna, since neither is the concrete trade meant here.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p508/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The command to witness transactions was discussed at the beginning of the verse.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p508/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · طاوس والحسن وقتادة وابن زيد | reports | One reading prohibits harming a scribe or witness through falsifying or altering the record, bearing false testimony, or refusing to testify; the active form has the writer and witness as agents.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p508/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن مسعود وعطاء ومجاهد | reports | Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAṭāʾ, and Mujāhid instead say not to summon a busy scribe or witness when attending would harm him; on this reading the verb is passive.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p508/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الزجاج | prefers | Al-Zajjāj chooses the first interpretation because fisq suits a false witness or person who alters writing, not someone who merely summoned a busy witness; defenders of the second read fisq as sin and disobedience.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p508/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · عمر وأبي وابن مسعود ومجاهد | reports | A reading attributed to ʿUmar, Ubayy, Ibn Masʿūd, and Mujāhid vocalizes the verb as passive, supporting the interpretation that a busy witness must not be burdened.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:281-282/r10] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The ban on harming a scribe or witness forbids altering records, false testimony, and refusing to testify; doing so is sinful.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:281-282/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | After prohibiting usury, God permits forward-credit sales and commands writing and witnessing deferred debts to protect property; the trust exception in 2:283 abrogates this command. | mentions 2:283
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:281-282/r3] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | A just scribe writes without altering amount or term and must not refuse when asked; this was first obligatory for writer and witness, then abrogated by the prohibition on harming them.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:281-282/r4] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | “As God taught him” recognizes God’s favor of literacy; the debtor dictates because he is liable and must acknowledge the debt aloud without reducing it.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:281-282/r5] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | A child, incapacitated fool, mute, or speech-impaired debtor has a guardian—an heir or representative—dictate truthfully on his behalf.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:281-282/r6] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Witnesses are two free adult men of the believers, acceptable for their merit and religion; if one woman forgets, the other reminds her of the testimony.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:281-282/r7] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Witnesses must not refuse when summoned to bear or give testimony; parties should not let irritation keep them from recording a small or large debt through its due date.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:281-282/r8] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Writing is fairest before God, makes testimony more reliable because the record reminds witnesses, and best prevents doubt about amount or due date.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:281-282/r9] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | An immediate exchange of goods is exempt from writing because the risks of delayed payment are absent; witnessing spot sales is also no longer obligatory under the abrogated ruling.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p17/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | In the travel poem, أطراف suggests both varied strands of conversation and the allusive gestures of companions; it conveys their lively ease, friendship, and pleasure on the journey home.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p17/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The poet says the camels' necks because speed and slowness show especially in their necks and heads, whose movement reveals their spirited gait.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p17/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Poetic excellence cannot be assigned to isolated words: unlike a jewel's intrinsic beauty, the relevant analogy is meanings enhancing one another through composition and relation.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p227/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Although tamthīl, simile, and metaphor are only three labels, explaining their divisions and fine distinctions requires extensive reading and thought; Jurjānī defends that detailed inquiry against dismissive critics.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p329/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Jurjānī endorses al-Āmidī’s view that rain's fashioning and weaving of plants is literal, not metaphor; al-Āmidī praises al-Buḥturī's phrasing and calls Abū Tammām's explicit weaver comparison ugly.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p329/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Jurjānī explains that explicit simile names both subjects, while implicit simile transfers the comparison's name to its subject; the same distinction lets actions be compared explicitly or called swimming and flight metaphorically.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p329/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | In the Abū Dulāma example, Jurjānī maps each mule leg's unstable or curved movement to a specific hand motion in kneading or baking dough.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p359/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · معترض | reports | An interlocutor objects that calling a brave man a lion does not transfer the word outside its meaning, since the intended comparison is courage, already associated with lions.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p359/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Jurjānī replies that lion includes bodily shape and visible traits as well as courage; applying its name to a man strips away those literal traits and transfers the name by an imagined likeness.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p359/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | By contrast, attributing an action to spring is literal: the language predicates an act without asserting anything about the subject's nature, so no part of the word's meaning is displaced.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p153/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | ‘You are the beloved’ presents love as a whole genus confined to one person, implying the speaker loves no one else; ‘Zayd, the one departing’ identifies a single known departure instead.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p153/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Adding a habitual quality, as in ‘Zayd who goes about your need’, makes the description generic and restores the genus-like sense found in ‘you are the beloved’.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p153/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A class noun becomes a distinct type when qualified; this applies both to ordinary nouns and to verbal nouns such as knowledge, striking, travel, and standing.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p153/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A verbal noun also divides into types through its complement: striking with a sword differs from striking with a stick, despite sharing the name ‘striking’.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p176/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Coordinated clauses need related subjects and reports; pairing Abu al-Husayn’s generosity with the bitterness of separation is jarring because the ideas have no connection.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p176/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | When clauses concern one person, the conjunction clearly asserts both actions together; without it, the second statement could retract the first.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p176/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Coordination inside a relative or similarly linked construction tightens the pairing further, so the actions cannot sensibly be understood apart.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p18/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Composed speech is built from grammatical relations, chiefly a noun with its predicate or a verb with its subject; further syntax adds qualifications or extensions.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p18/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The poem challenges anyone who reduces nazm to shared grammar to explain how that account can establish the Qur’an’s unmatched inimitability.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p263/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | With ‘not ... except’, placing the predicate after the subject restricts the predicate to that subject, while placing the predicate first restricts the subject to those bearing that predicate.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p263/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | ‘Zayd is nothing but standing’ excludes incompatible states such as sitting, but does not exclude unrelated qualities such as being tall, white, or learned; ‘no one is standing but Zayd’ is context-bound.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p263/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The restriction denies that another, incompatible state replaces the named one, rather than denying all accompanying attributes; unlike ‘innamā’, ‘mā ... illā’ already excludes every contrary state.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p297/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A word is not eloquent in isolation: the same word can be excellent in one context and ordinary elsewhere because its merit appears only after it enters a composition.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p297/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Though ordinary usage calls words eloquent rather than meanings, the claim that eloquence lies in meaning means that the merit behind an eloquent word ultimately returns to its meaning.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p297/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Since a speaker cannot alter linguistic words or add a new formal quality to them, while eloquence is the speaker’s achiev

[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p310/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · القائلون | reports | Critics argue that one meaning can be expressed in two ways, one eloquent and one not; this would give words an independent share in excellence.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p310/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | rejects | If the comparison concerns synonymous individual words, it misses the issue: Jurjānī is discussing eloquence produced by composition, not isolated vocabulary.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p310/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | If it concerns whole expressions, the same basic meaning can be plain or artistically fashioned, like a simple piece of jewelry versus an expertly crafted one.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p311/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The commonplace thought that nature cannot change becomes newly striking in al-Mutanabbī’s line, where nature resists being carried away.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p311/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | An eloquent expression improves and adorns a shared underlying meaning, giving it a distinctive image that a plain paraphrase lacks.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p311/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | If a critic admits the added beauty in the poetic examples, the excellence lies in the newly shaped meaning, not in the letters’ sound; denying it makes discussion futile.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p321/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A parable’s purpose is inferred from the combined sense, not from literal words: a ruler’s image of advancing one foot and drawing back the other means wavering over whether to pledge allegiance.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p321/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The Prophet’s ‘green plants of dung heaps’ figures a beautiful woman of poor upbringing, just as ‘much ash in the pot’ figures generous hospitality; the inferred meaning, not the phrase, is the parable.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p64/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The source of eloquence and inimitability is the arrangement of meanings, not the order of bare words; a word-focused account of the Qur’an’s merit collapses.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p64/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Fasāḥa is attributed to a word because it names the quality by which that word signals rhetorical merit; the meaning itself is not directly described as eloquent.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p64/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Older critics’ ‘noble’ or ‘restless’ word is shorthand for semantic fit with neighboring meanings: wording is called settled or awkward because of what it conveys in the composition.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p76/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Jurjānī says scholars agree that nazm is indispensable to eloquent speech; without it, unusual meanings alone confer no rank or completeness.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p76/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Nazm means arranging speech as grammar requires, following its rules and distinctions rather than merely placing words in sequence.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p76/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The composer must consider the different forms available within each grammatical category, such as alternative word orders and predicate forms.

[JISHUMI:v2p1070#2/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · العامة | reports | The common reading has the imperative lām in وليكتب with sukūn.
[JISHUMI:v2p1070#2/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · زيد بن أسلم | reports | Zayd ibn Aslam reads فتذاكر with an alif, as reciprocal discussion.
[JISHUMI:v2p1070#2/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan reads the lām in وليكتب with kasra.
[JISHUMI:v2p1070#2/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The lām is an imperative; when preceded by waw, fa, or thumma, most Arabs give it sukūn for ease, while others preserve its original kasra.
[JISHUMI:v2p1070#2/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza reads the hamza of إن with kasra and فتذكر with indicative mood and shadda; he construes the phrase conditionally and as a new clause after the conditional fa.
[JISHUMI:v2p1070#2/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | In Ḥamza’s reading, تضل is jussive in the conditional though its doubling obscures the form; فتذكر is indicative as the clause after the conditional fa begins anew.
[JISHUMI:v2p1070#2/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الباقون | reports | The other readers use fatḥ on أن and read فتذكر in connection with the preceding clause, with نصب either as the object of the verb or after an understood preposition أن.
[JISHUMI:v2p1070#2/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · نافع وعاصم والكسائي وابن عامر | reports | Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, and Ibn ʿĀmir read فتذكر with shadda and نصب; Ḥamza uses shadda and رفع, while Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr use a light form with نصب.
[JISHUMI:v2p1070#2/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The light and doubled forms are both Arabic usage, like dhakkara/adhkara and nazzala/anzala.
[JISHUMI:v2p1070#2/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · عاصم والجحدري | reports | ʿĀṣim and al-Jaḥdarī read تضل with passive morphology, ḍamma on the yāʾ and fatḥ on the ḍād.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · العامة | reports | The common reading uses second-person feminine/masculine address in لا تسأموا.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Imlāʾ and imlāl are two forms for dictating; imlāl fundamentally means repeating something again and again. | mentions 25:5
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Bakhṣ means unjustly diminishing something, as in depriving someone of his due. | mentions 12:20
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Safah means ignorance, with its root sense being lightness; the term describes a lightness of intellect.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Saʾam means weariness or boredom, becoming annoyed with something.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Ḍalāl originally means destruction; Arabic says water was lost in milk, and the Qurʾan also uses it for the criminals' ruin. | mentions 54:47
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Another proposed root sense of ḍalāl is going away so completely that one cannot be found, as in the question about being lost in the earth. | mentions 32:10
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r16] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Ibaʾ means refusing or refraining from something, as in Iblis's refusal. | mentions 2:34
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r17] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Qisṭ means justice and derives from turning toward the truth; aqsaṭa describes acting justly.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r18] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Adnā derives from nearness and means closer; al-dunyā is named for being nearer than the hereafter.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r19] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Irtiyāb is doubt arising from suspicion.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · السلمي | reports | Al-Sulami reads لا يسأموا with yāʾ, referring back to the preceding past context.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r20] JISHUMI, d. 494 · علي بن عيسى | reports | Ali ibn ʿIsa gives four sound expansions for the nominative phrase: let there be witnesses, let a man and two women testify, the witnesses are these, or they testify.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r21] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | The phrase may instead be accusative, with an implied command to summon one man and two women as witnesses.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · عاصم | reports | Asim reads تجارة in the accusative as the predicate of كان, with an omitted subject: unless the trade is a trade.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | For the nominative reading, one analysis supplies تقع: unless a trade occurs.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Another nominative analysis makes تجارة the subject of كان and the following clause its predicate, meaning a trade circulating among you.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abu Jaʿfar reads يضار in the jussive with a light, ungeminated rāʾ.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan reads يضار with a kasra and a geminated rāʾ.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · العامة | reports | The common reading has the accusative and gemination; its form derives from لا تضارر with two r's assimilated.
[JISHUMI:v2p1071/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Al-dayn is an obligation established in the debtor's liability, and al-ajal is the appointed time, or the time's end.
[JISHUMI:v2p1073/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh explains that straying is stated before reminding because it causes the reminder; the connected actions function as one purpose, as in propping a wall because it is leaning.

1073/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | An alternative construction supplies the omitted preposition من: do not tire of writing it.
[JISHUMI:v2p1073/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The pronoun in تكتبوه refers to the debt/right owed.
[JISHUMI:v2p1073/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ takes the phrase conditionally: one woman reminds the other if she strays; fronting أن makes it attach to the preceding governor.
[JISHUMI:v2p1073/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | The pronoun in إلى أجله may refer to the debt's term or to the witness's term of eligibility; the debt's term is the stronger reading.
[JISHUMI:v2p1073/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الحسن، وقتادة، وابن زيد | reports | The kasra reading of يضارر is associated with al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd.
[JISHUMI:v2p1073/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن مسعود ومجاهد | reports | Ibn Masʿud and Mujahid are associated with the fatḥa reading, meaning a witness must not be summoned while occupied in order to harm him.
[JISHUMI:v2p1073/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The two r's assimilate; the form is accusative because of gemination and the meeting of two sukūns, with fatḥa chosen as the lightest vowel.
[JISHUMI:v2p1073/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The final two lām letters remain distinct because the second is still quiescent in the imperative; when the lām is made mobile, as in يمل, assimilation occurs.
[JISHUMI:v2p1073/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Tartābū is on the tafaʿʿal pattern from rayba; its original yāʾ moved after a fatḥa and changed into a long alif.
[JISHUMI:v2p1073/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The clause after أن is accusative either as an infinitive meaning its writing, or after deletion of the preposition من.
[JISHUMI:v2p1074/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The phrase can be parsed as a circumstantial clause, or as a predicate of an elided كان: ‘whether the debt is small or large.’
[JISHUMI:v2p1074/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | After forbidding usury, God permits salam and debts; after commanding respite, he also commands fulfillment before documentation and witnesses.
[JISHUMI:v2p1074/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Jishumi glosses the address as a call to affirm God and his messenger.
[JISHUMI:v2p1074/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Tadayantum means that people deal with one another by lending or incurring a debt.
[JISHUMI:v2p1074/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The word ‘debt’ is repeated because tadaayantum can mean either mutual repayment or dealings involving debt, so the repetition disambiguates the shared expression.
[JISHUMI:v2p1074/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The repetition also reinforces the meaning in the mind, as in the emphatic Qur’anic phrases about the angels prostrating and birds flying with wings. | mentions 15:30, 38:73, 6:38
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | A specified term is a stated and known time.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الشعبي وجماعة من المفسرين | prefers | Al-Shaʿbī and other exegetes say writing is a communal obligation, like jihad; Jishumi says this is the view followed in practice.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī says the duty applies to the scribe when he is free to write.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · مجاهد وعطاء والربيع | reports | Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, and al-Rabīʿ say writing is obligatory when the scribe is asked.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Some say the command that a scribe not refuse was abrogated by the instruction not to harm a scribe or witness; the adopted practice is the first view, communal obligation.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Writing is emphasized because scribes were few in the Prophet’s time.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The debtor should dictate by acknowledging in his own words what he owes, so the amount due is known.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r16] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The debtor must avoid disobeying God’s command and must not reduce any part of the debt.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r17] JISHUMI, d. 494 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid glosses safīh as someone ignorant about dictation.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r18] JISHUMI, d. 494 · السدي والضحاك | reports | Al-Suddī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk gloss safīh as a young child.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r19] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd glosses safīh as incapable or foolish.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse was revealed specifically about salam sales.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r20] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Weak is explained as sick or senile with age; unable to dictate includes muteness, foreign speech, or similar inability.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r21] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | Jishumi says the three categories should be understood as distinct to avoid repetition: mentally disabled, young, and unable to dictate, with comparable cases included under each.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r22] JISHUMI, d. 494 · القاضي | reports | The Qāḍī’s preferred mapping is a spendthrift for safīh, an adolescent child for weak, and an insane person as unable to dictate; each label may include equivalents.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r23] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الضحاك وابن زيد | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd say the guardian of the incompetent person dictates what that person owes, acting in his place.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r24] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس والربيع ومقاتل | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Rabīʿ, and Muqātil identify the guardian as the creditor, who knows the debt and dictates it fairly.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r25] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The instruction is to seek witnesses and have them testify to the written record; two men suffice generally, except that adultery requires four.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r26] JISHUMI, d. 494 · مجاهد وجماعة من الفقهاء | reports | Mujāhid and many jurists restrict the male witnesses to free, adult Muslims, excluding non-Muslims, slaves, and children.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r27] JISHUMI, d. 494 · شريح وابن سيرين | reports | Shurayḥ and Ibn Sīrīn permit testimony by slaves.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r28] JISHUMI, d. 494 · مالك | reports | Mālik permits children’s testimony in cases of assault injuries.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r29] JISHUMI, d. 494 · مالك والأوزاعي والشافعي | reports | Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, and al-Shāfiʿī restrict the male-and-two-women arrangement to financial matters.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · المفسرون والفقهاء | prefers | The exegetes and jurists apply the verse to every debt and sale price, whether the sold item is delivered now or later.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r30] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أهل العراق | reports | Iraqi jurists apply it to all matters except fixed criminal penalties and retaliation.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r31] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Acceptable witnesses are upright in religion, trustworthy, and competent; another gloss requires that no suspicion or accusation attach to them.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r32] JISHUMI, d. 494 · إبراهيم | reports | Ibrāhīm defines an acceptable witness as someone who has not shown cause for suspicion.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r33] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbī describes a trustworthy witness as one not accused in matters of appetite or sexual conduct.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r34] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الربيع والسدي والضحاك وابن زيد | reports | Al-Rabīʿ, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Zayd, and most exegetes take ‘go astray’ as forget, so one woman reminds the other of the testimony.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r35] JISHUMI, d. 494 · سفيان بن عيينة | reports | Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna instead understands the reminder as making one woman like a male witness.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r36] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | rejects | Jishumi rejects the ‘make her like a man’ gloss because the preceding condition that one may err indicates that reminder means recalling the testimony.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Mussammā means that the term is stated and known.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Writing down the debt prevents later forgetfulness or denial.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو سعيد الخدري والحسن | reports | Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and al-Ḥasan, with most scholars, treat writing the debt as recommended.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الربيع وكعب | reports | Al-Rabīʿ and Kaʿb regard writing the debt as obligatory.
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbī reports that writing, witnessing, and pledging were once obligatory and were abrogated by the following verse’s allowance when parties trust each other; Jishumi prefers the view that writing is recommended as a means of securing rights. | mentions 2:283
[JISHUMI:v2p1075/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The scribe records the debt or sale between the parties with fairness, neither adding nor subtracting nor harming either without their knowledge.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · مجاهد وعطاء والشعبي والسدي وسعيد بن جبير | prefers | Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Shaʿbī, al-Suddī, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr take the call as one to give testimony in court; the Qāḍī chooses this view.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الحسن والشافعي | prefers | Al-Ḥasan and al-Shāfiʿī regard witnessing sales as recommended, which Jishumi says is the jurists’ position.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | On the active reading, the underlying form is yudārir with kasra; the writer and witness are the agents.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · عطاء وطاووس والحسن وقتادة وابن زيد | reports | The writer must not be harmed by being forbidden to write or made to add or subtract from what was dictated; the witness must not be made to refuse or testify to what he does not know.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | On the passive reading, the writer and witness are the objects of harm.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | The passive reading means not to burden a writer or witness whe

[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | The forbidden conduct is understood as harming the writer and witness or doing what was prohibited and disobeying what was commanded; it is departure from God’s obedience.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r16] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Taqwā here means avoiding disobedience and sin, or safeguarding trusts by discharging them.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r17] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | God teaches people what benefits them in religious and worldly affairs, which they did not know.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r18] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | God’s knowledge is glossed as universal, knowledge of people’s deeds and recompense, or knowledge of their interests that informs his commands and prohibitions.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس والحسن | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan understand the call to cover both bearing and giving testimony.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | rejects | Some reject interpreting the call as bearing testimony because the people have not yet become witnesses; Jishumi answers that the command to seek two witnesses makes them witnesses.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | If the verse concerns bearing testimony, that duty is variously described as communal obligation, recommendation, or permission; if giving testimony, it is communal when others can do it and individual when no substitute exists.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Do not tire of documenting the debt, whether small or large, and continue through its due date; another view refers to the witness’s term.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | The term is explained as the due date of the debt or, alternatively, the witness’s term.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The writing is more just before God because he commanded it, and obeying his command is more just than leaving it; it is also sounder for testimony and nearer to removing doubt.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The exception is an immediate cash sale, hand to hand, with no deferred term; documenting it is not required and causes no harm or financial burden.
[JISHUMI:v2p1077/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk considers witnessing a sale obligatory.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Jurists unanimously permit debts in fungible goods such as currency, wheat, and barley.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The verse prescribes fair drafting of contract terms and documents and forbids harming either party.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The scribe must have enough expertise to distinguish fair documentation from unfair terms.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The debtor must acknowledge the debt and bear witness against himself; the parties need document only enough testimony for reliable assurance.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The incapacity clauses identify cases that prevent a valid acknowledgment by the debtor.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Acknowledgments are accepted and acted upon, and testimony can be given about them just as about deferred debts.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The acknowledgment of an incapable or weak debtor is not accepted; his guardian dictates in his place.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r16] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | Some treat foolishness, weakness, and inability as three distinct causes; others treat them as one condition, with a guardian dictating in either case.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r17] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | There is no disagreement that a minor or an insane person's acknowledgment is invalid.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r18] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أهل العراق | reports | Iraqi jurists accept the acknowledgment of a financially profligate person after interdiction.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r19] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi‘i does not accept a profligate person's acknowledgment after interdiction.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الأكثر | reports | Most jurists disallow deferred debt in nonfungible goods such as animals and clothing.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r20] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | The author construes the foolish debtor as insane, the weak as a minor, and the unable speaker as mute or similarly unable.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · بعضهم | reports | Some jurists permit deferred debt in nonfungible goods.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Jurists agree that obligations owed on liability may have a deferred term; specific assets cannot be deferred.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The term must be known: that is the force of specified, and an unknown term defeats the purpose of writing and witnessing.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | Writing and witnessing are guidance and recommendation, not obligation, since a creditor may waive the right itself and need not document it as a precaution.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | Another view makes writing a collective duty when a group is present, and an individual duty when only one writer is available.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The debt cannot be demanded before its due date; otherwise specifying a term would have no effect.
[JISHUMI:v2p1078/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | A debt is legally due even though the demand for payment is deferred.
[JISHUMI:v2p1079/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The verse implies that rulers and judges must be appointed, since a fool's and a weak person's affairs cannot be managed without them.
[JISHUMI:v2p1079/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو يوسف | reports | In an anecdote before al-Muʿtadid's vizier, judge Abu Hazim cites Abu Yusuf's definition of integrity: avoid major sins and persistence in minor ones, show more concealment than scandal and more correctness than error, display muruʾa, and restrain from lying through piety or honor.
[JISHUMI:v2p1079/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أهل العراق | reports | Iraqi jurists accept the testimony of non-Muslims against one another; Malik and al-Shafiʿi do not.
[JISHUMI:v2p1079/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو علي وأكثر الفقهاء | prefers | Abu ʿAli and most jurists infer that judgment cannot rest on one witness plus an oath because that exceeds the divinely set limit; Abu Hashim and al-Shafiʿi permit it.
[JISHUMI:v2p1079/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The command identifies witnesses, their number, method, and qualifications, and indicates a duty to establish testimony.
[JISHUMI:v2p1079/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Taking witnesses is guidance and recommendation in ordinary transactions; most jurists require witnesses for marriage, though Malik does not.
[JISHUMI:v2p1079/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Jurists agree that witnesses are not required for divorce, while Abu Hanifa does not require them for revocation and al-Shafiʿi does.
[JISHUMI:v2p1079/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Two witnesses suffice for property claims, with no disagreement on this or on testimony in adultery cases.
[JISHUMI:v2p1079/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | For matters that are neither property, a prescribed punishment, nor a defined right, Abu Hanifa accepts women's testimony while al-Shafiʿi rejects it.
[JISHUMI:v2p1079/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Women alone may testify in matters men cannot observe, such as female defects, childbirth, and the newborn's first cry; jurists disagree about nursing.
