[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | If كما علمه الله attaches to أن يكتب, refusal of the specified writing is forbidden and that writing is commanded; if to فليكتب, refusal in general is forbidden, then qualified writing commanded.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | كما may attach to لا يأب causally: since God favored him with literacy, he should not refuse but write generously; the Sheikh calls this unlikely.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Even if كما attaches to فليكتب, its كاف can still be causal: he should write because God taught him.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · العامة | reports | The general reading has a silent lām in فليكتب, treating the separate word like a connected word; al-Hasan reads its original kasra.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | وليملل is the command of أمل يمِل; with the second radical jussive, Hijazis use dissimilation and Tamimis assimilation, including in pause; وليمل is an anomalous assimilated reading.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | أمل and أملى both mean dictating; some call them dialects, others derive the yāʾ as a replacement for a doubled consonant, with repetition underlying both forms. | mentions 5:54
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | الحق may be a subject with عليه as a fronted predicate, or a subject governed by the preceding preposition; the relative debtor is the subject of يملل and its two objects are understood.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The implied meaning is that the debtor dictates the written amount due to the writer; أمللت عليه takes على with one of its objects.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#5/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | منه attaches to يبخس, with من marking origin and the pronoun referring to the debt; alternatively it is an omitted adjective of an indefinite, fronted as a circumstantial.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#5/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | شيئا may be a direct object or cognate accusative; بخس means decrease, originally of a damaged eye, metaphorically applied to a right, with بخص as a variant.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#5/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | reports | هو confirms the implicit subject of يمل to remove figurative attribution and specify that the debtor cannot dictate personally.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#5/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | rejects | The Sheikh calls the silent-hāʾ reading in هو more anomalous than ثم هو يوم القيامة; the author rejects that judgment. | mentions 28:6
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#5/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The silent-hāʾ form is not anomalous: it is mutawatir from Nafi through Qalun and from al-Kisa'i.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#5/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The pronoun in وليه refers to the debtor when he has one of the three stated limitations; بالعدل repeats the earlier construction.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#6/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | استشهدوا may retain the request sense of استفعل, or استفعل may mean أفعل, as in استعجل/أعجل and استيقن/أيقن.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#6/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The intensive form شهيدين suggests choosing witnesses who testify repeatedly.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#6/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | من رجالكم may attach to استشهدوا with من marking source, or be an adjective of شهيدين with partitive من.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#6/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | If كان is incomplete, its dual subject refers to the two witnesses: if the creditor fails or chooses not to secure two men, the alternative applies.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#6/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | If كان is complete, رجلين is an emphatic circumstantial: the alternative is used only when two male witnesses cannot be found.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#7/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | فرجل وامرأتان may be a subject with an omitted predicate such as sufficient for testimony, a predicate of an omitted subject الشاهد, or a nominative with an omitted verb.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#7/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | prefers | Al-Zamakhshari supplies فليشهد رجل, meaning let a man and two women testify; this avoids deleting a construct noun and is the best analysis.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#7/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | Other analyses make the phrase a subject of complete or incomplete كان, or passive فليستشهد رجل; complete كان is preferable because it requires fewer deletions.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#7/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa notes that an accusative reading would imply فاستشهدوا.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#7/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A reading gives وامرأتان with a silent hamza; one account treats the hamza as replaced by alif and then rehamzat, though that is not its regular softening.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#7/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa explains the silent hamza as first softened between hamza and alif, then treated as alif and rehamzat, as in عألم and خأتم.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#7/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A second account silences hamza because successive vowels burden it; a poet's أنا after waw is offered as a parallel.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#8/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن جني | rejects | Ibn Jinni rules out silencing hamza because fatḥa is light; the author says this generalization ignores other poetic, prose, and readi

[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#8/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | ممن ترضون may be a nominative adjective of رجل وامرأتان; the Sheikh rejects this because it would exclude the two male witnesses.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#8/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | It may instead be an accusative adjective of شهيدين; Abu al-Baqa rejects this because intervening words separate adjective and noun.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#8/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | It may be apposition to من رجالكم with the preposition repeated; the Sheikh objects that apposition would still restrict the phrase to the men.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#8/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | prefers | The Sheikh attaches ممن ترضون directly to استشهدوا so the qualification applies to every witness; its late position signals this scope.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#9/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | من الشهداء may be a circumstantial of the omitted relative pronoun in ممن ترضون, or apposition to its من with a repeated preposition.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#9/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Hamza reads إن تضل as a conditional particle; others read أن تضل as an accusative verbal noun, with a causal lām understood.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#9/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · حمزة | reports | Hamza reads فتذكر with doubled kāf and nominative rāʾ as the conditional answer, understood as فهي تذكر.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#9/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya makes the conditional and answer a nominative adjective of the two women; the Sheikh objects to the awkward order and possible intervening phrase.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#9/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الواحدي | reports | Al-Wahidi had already proposed the conditional clause as an adjective of the two women, citing a relative clause followed by a condition and response. | mentions 22:41
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#9/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The apparent reading treats the conditional as an independent statement answering why two women are assigned in place of one man.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282#9/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | With أن, the verb is subjunctive and the lām of purpose is omitted: لأن تضل or إرادة أن تضل; its fatha differs from the junction fatha in Hamza's jussive reading.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | إلى أجل attaches to تداينتم; attaching it to an omitted adjective of دين is possible but weak because it fronts an interpreted adjective before an explicit one.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | تداين is reciprocal form of الدين, like تبايع from البيع; داينت means dealing in debt whether giving or taking, as in Ruʾbah's verse.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | دنت الرجل means selling to him on credit, while أدنته means borrowing from him; the two patterns differentiate the directions.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:282/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The pronoun in فاكتبوه returns to دين; that noun is repeated to provide an antecedent, disambiguate reciprocal تداينوا, or indicate every amount of debt.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p10/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | When an explanation is absent from the Qurʾan, Sunna, and Companions, many imams turn to the Successors; Ibn Kathīr names Mujāhid, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, ʿIkrima, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, and others.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p10/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid says he recited the entire muṣḥaf to Ibn ʿAbbās three times, stopping at every verse to ask its interpretation.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p10/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن أبي مليكة | reports | Ibn Abī Mulayka says he saw Mujāhid ask Ibn ʿAbbās for the Qurʾan’s interpretation with writing tablets; Ibn ʿAbbās told him to write until he had asked about all of it.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p10/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · سفيان الثوري | reports | Sufyān al-Thawrī regarded an interpretation transmitted from Mujāhid as sufficient.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p10/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Apparent differences in Successor wording often are not real disagreements: one may state an implication or equivalent, while another states the point directly.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p10/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · شعبة بن الحجاج | reports | Shuʿba b. al-Ḥajjāj and others argue that Successors’ legal opinions are not binding evidence for others, asking how they could be binding in tafsīr.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p10/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathīr agrees Successor opinions do not bind those who disagree, but consensus is evidence; where they differ, none overrides another, so consult Qurʾanic usage, Sunna, Arabic usage, and Companions’ views.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p10/r8] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · النبي | reports | A report from Ibn ʿAbbās attributes to the Prophet a warning that whoever interprets the Qurʾan by opinion or without knowledge should take his seat in the Fire; Ibn Kathīr cites it to prohibit such tafsīr.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p19/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The messenger between God and Muḥammad was Gabriel, a noble and honored angel; Ibn Kathīr says God praised both Gabriel and Muḥammad and cites descriptions of them in the Qurʾan. | mentions 26:193, 26:194, 81:19, 81:20, 81:21, 81:22
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p19/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathīr notes a virtue for Umm Salama, who saw Gabriel, and for the handsome Dihya b. Khalīfa al-Kalbī, whose appearance Gabriel often assumed when visiting the Prophet.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p19/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | reports | Dihya and Usāma b. Zayd were affiliated with Kalb b. Wabara of Quḍāʿa; Quḍāʿa was variously said to descend from ʿAdnān, from Qaḥṭān, or to be an independent branch, and Ibn Kathīr leaves the matter to God.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p19/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying every prophet received a sign by which people believed, while Muḥammad’s gift was revelation from God; he hopes to have the greatest following on Resurrection Day, and Ibn Kathīr notes its transmission by al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and al-Nasāʾī.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p23/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أنس بن مالك | reports | Anas reports that ʿUthmān assigned Zayd, Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ, Ibn al-Zubayr, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. al-Ḥārith to copy codices, directing them to use Quraysh speech if they and Zayd differed in Qurʾanic Arabic.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p23/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathīr says al-Bukhārī’s point is that the Qurʾan was revealed in Quraysh’s language, and Quraysh were the foremost branch of the Arabs.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p23/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | ʿUmar reportedly said only Qurashī or Thaqafī youths should dictate in the official codices; Ibn Kathīr grades the chain ṣaḥīḥ.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p23/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | Another report says ʿUmar instructed his committee to use the language of Muḍar when linguistic differences arose, because the Qurʾan came in the language of a man from Muḍar, the Prophet.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p23/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathīr cites verses describing the Qurʾan as Arabic and revealed in clear Arabic as evidence for its language, also citing the challenge about a non-Arabic Qurʾan. | mentions 39:28, 26:192, 26:193, 26:194, 26:195, 16:103, 41:44
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p23/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · يعلى بن أمية | reports | Yaʿlā b. Umayya wished to witness revelation; when a man in iḥrām wearing perfume and a cloak asked about ʿumra, ʿUmar brought Yaʿlā close to observe the Prophet receive revelation, after which the Prophet ordered the cloak removed and perfume washed away.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p27#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · حذيفة بن اليمان | reports | During the Armenia and Azerbaijan campaigns, Ḥudhayfa heard Syrian and Iraqi Muslims differing in their recitations and warned ʿUthmān to act before the community divided over scripture as Jews and Christians had.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p27#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عثمان بن عفان | reports | ʿUthmān borrowed Ḥafṣa’s pages and commissioned Zayd ibn Thābit, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith to copy them into codices.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p27#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عثمان بن عفان | reports | ʿUthmān instructed the three Qurashī copyists to use Quraysh’s speech whenever they and Zayd disagreed, because the Qur’an was revealed in that dialect; the official copies were sent to the regions and other codices burned.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p27#2/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · زيد بن ثابت | reports | Zayd says the copyists noticed a verse missing from al-Aḥzāb that he had heard the Prophet recite; they found it with Khuzayma ibn Thābit and inserted it in its sūra. | mentions 33:23
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p27#2/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir counts ʿUthmān’s unification of the community on one reading among his greatest merits; Abū Bakr and ʿUmar had earlier collected the Qur’an to prevent any part from being lost.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p27#2/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The Companions all agreed with ʿUthmān’s decision; Ibn Masʿūd initially showed anger because he was not among the codex copyists and told his followers to conceal their codices, but later returned to agreement.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p27#2/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | ʿAlī said that had ʿUthmān not taken this step, he would have done it himself.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p27#2/r8] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet’s instruction to follow his Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs in support of their united decision.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p32/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · مصعب بن سعد | reports | Musʿab b. Saʿd reports that ʿUthmān responded to reading disputes by collecting written Qurʾan fragments, checking each against the Prophet’s dictation, assigning Saʿīd to dictate a

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p32/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · كثير بن أفلح | reports | Kathīr b. Aflah reports that ʿUthmān assembled twelve Qurashī and Anṣārī men, including Ubayy and Zayd, and brought the collected sheets; Ibn Kathīr calls this report ṣaḥīḥ.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p32/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · محمد بن سيرين | reports | Ibn Sīrīn conjectures that the group delayed disputed material so they could identify who had most recently heard the final presentation and write accordingly.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p32/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathīr clarifies that the collected sheets were with Ḥafṣa; ʿUthmān used them to compile the codex, then returned them to her as promised rather than burning them.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p32/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | After Ḥafṣa died, Marwān b. al-Ḥakam took and burned the sheets, adopting the rationale ʿUthmān had used for destroying other copies.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p45/r10] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites Ibn ʿAbbās, who says he learned فاطر from an Arab describing a well he had begun digging as one he had fathomed or started. | mentions 35:1
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p45/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الطحاوي | reports | Al-Ṭaḥāwī and others explain the seven-language allowance as a concession because many people struggled with Quraysh speech, lacking writing, precise notation, and secure memorization.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p45/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الطحاوي والقاضي الباقلاني وأبو عمرو بن عبد البر | reports | Al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-Bāqillānī, and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr hold that the early concession to recite in seven dialects was later abrogated once hardship ended and memorization, precision, and writing spread.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p45/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · بعضهم | reports | One view says ʿUthmān consolidated the community on one reading and final recension because variation risked division and mutual accusations of unbelief, then prohibited other readings despite the former concession.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p45/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | reports | The same account compares ʿUthmān’s action with ʿUmar enforcing triple divorce after its repeated use, restricting pilgrimage-season tamattuʿ to keep visits to the Kaʿba from being confined to pilgrimage months, and Abū Mūsā’s obedience in ceasing his fatwa.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p45/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الخطابي | reports | A second view says the Qurʾan’s seven aḥruf do not mean every passage is recited in all seven; different passages may occur in different forms. Al-Khaṭṭābī gives 5:60 and 12:12 as examples. | mentions 5:60, 12:12
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p45/r8] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو عبيد | reports | Al-Qurṭubī says Abū ʿUbayd held this distributed-form view and Ibn ʿAṭiyya selected it; Abū ʿUbayd adds that some dialects fit particular expressions better than others.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p45/r9] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · القاضي الباقلاني | reports | Al-Bāqillānī says ʿUthmān’s statement that it was revealed in Quraysh speech means most of it, not all: no proof establishes that every word is Qurashī, since Arabic includes all tribes; Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr agrees.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p65#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عبد الله بن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar reports the Prophet’s saying that only two cases merit envy: a person given scripture who recites through the night and a wealthy person who gives charity night and day; al-Bukhārī alone transmits this route, while both Ṣaḥīḥs include a Sufyān route from al-Zuhrī.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p65#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet’s parallel saying: one taught the Qurʾan recites it night and day, and one given wealth spends it for the right; neighbors wish they could do likewise.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p721#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | This is the longest verse in the Qur'an; Ibn Shihab says he was told it was the latest Qur'anic verse revealed at the Throne.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p721#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | A Prophetic report says Adam first denied an agreement: God showed him his descendants, including David, gave David forty years from Adam's thousand-year lifespan, and documented and witnessed the gift; Adam later denied it until shown the record. A version says David lived one hundred and Adam completed one thousand. Ibn Kathir calls the report very strange and notes weakness in Ali ibn Zayd's narrations, though al-Hakim gives variants through Abu Hurayra.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p721#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Writing deferred transactions is guidance that better preserves the amount and due date and keeps the testimony accurate, as the verse's stated rationale explains.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p722/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Through Mujahid, Ibn Abbas says the verse was revealed concerning salam, an advance payment due at a known term.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p722/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas swears that deferred forward sale for a specified term is permitted by God and reads this verse as evidence; al-Bukhari transmits it.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p722/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | When people in Medina paid in advance for fruit deliveries two or three years ahead, the Prophet instructed that advance sales specify a known measure, weight, and term; the report is in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p723#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir calls the preceding loan story's chain sound and says al-Bukhari narrated it in seven sound routes, sometimes through 'Abd Allah ibn Salih from al-Layth.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p723#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | A writer must record fairly and justly, without bias or adding to or reducing the agreed terms.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p723#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Someone who knows how to write should not refuse a request; writing for those unable to do so is charity, as supported by reports about helping a worker and concealing knowledge.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p723#2/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · مجاهد وعطاء | reports | They hold that it is obligatory for a capable writer to write.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p723/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Writing is ordered for documentation and preservation, not because religion itself requires writing: Qur'an and Sunna are made easy to memorize. Specific transactions should be written as guidance, not obligation, according to one view, reconciling the instruction with the report that the community neither writes nor calculates.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p723/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن جريج | reports | He says a borrower should write down a debt and a buyer should have witnesses.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p723/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · قتادة | reports | He recounts Abu Sulayman al-Mar'ashi's warning: a seller who grants credit without writing or witnesses and is later cheated has wronged himself by disobeying God, so his plea is not answered.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p723/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو سعيد والشعبي والربيع بن أنس والحسن وابن جريج وابن زيد | reports | They hold that writing transactions was initially obligatory, then abrogated by the option to trust one another and discharge the entrusted obligation in 2:283. | mentions 2:283
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p723/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو هريرة | reports | A Prophetic story tells of an Israelite borrower who could find no ship to repay a thousand dinars, placed the money and a note in a sealed log, and entrusted it to the sea after invoking God as witness and guarantor; the lender found it, and the borrower later came with repayment too.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p724#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The condition that witnesses be approved implies their probity; al-Shafi'i uses it to specify other unqualified Qur'anic witness commands, and some use it to reject unknown-status witnesses.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p724#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | If one woman forgets, the other reminds her; another reading intensifies the verb. Ibn Kathir rejects the claim that having two women together makes them equivalent to a man and prefers the reminder interpretation.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p724#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · قتادة والربيع بن أنس | reports | They interpret 'when called' as a summons to undertake testimony, which witnesses must accept; this makes taking testimony a communal obligation.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p724#2/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الجمهور | prefers | The majority interprets the summons as one to give testimony already borne; a witness must answer when personally required, otherwise the duty is communal.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p724#2/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · مجاهد وأبو مجلز | reports | If invited to take testimony, one may choose; after having witnessed, one must respond when called to testify.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p724#2/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · زيد بن خالد | reports | A Prophetic report calls the best witnesses those who bring their testimony before being asked for it.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p724#2/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Other reports condemn witnesses who testify before being asked, whose oaths and testimony precede each other, or who testify without a request; these are false witnesses.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p724/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The debtor dictates the debt and must fear God, withholding none of it; if the debtor is wasteful and legally restricted, young, insane, or unable to dictate through speech difficulty or ignorance, the guardian dictates fairly.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p724/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Witnesses accompany writing for additional assurance. In financial matters, one man and two women may test

ify; Ibn Kathir connects this arrangement to a hadith describing women's testimony as half a man's and explaining their lesser reason and religious practice.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p725/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Do not grow weary of recording a debt, large or small, through its due date; writing deferred claims is more just before God, strengthens testimony by helping witnesses remember, and reduces doubt in disputes.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p725/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الشعبي والحسن | reports | They say the command to witness sales was abrogated by the option to trust one another and return the entrusted property in 2:283. | mentions 2:283
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p725/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الجمهور | prefers | The majority treats witnessing sales as guidance and recommendation, not obligation; the report of the Prophet's disputed horse purchase and Khuzaima's extraordinary testimony supports this.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p726#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الحسن وقتادة | reports | They understand the prohibition as forbidding a writer from recording anything contrary to what was dictated or a witness from falsely testifying or concealing testimony.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p726#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Another interpretation forbids burdening or harming the writer and witness: a person summons them, and they explain that they are occupied, but he insists that they were commanded to answer; Ibn Abbas says the caller may not harm them. [IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p726/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i transmit the horse-purchase story through other routes from al-Zuhri, supporting the report about Khuzaima's testimony.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p726/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو موسى | reports | A report says prayers are not answered for three: a man who keeps a badly behaved wife without divorcing her, a guardian who gives an orphan's wealth before maturity, and a lender who lends without witnesses. [IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p726/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir says witnessing remains the prudent safeguard.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p727/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Disobeying these directions and doing what was forbidden is an abiding sin from which people cannot escape.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p727/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Fearing God means keeping watch, following His commands, and leaving His prohibitions; the promise that God teaches those who fear Him is compared with the discernment of 8:29 and light from 57:28. | mentions 8:29, 57:28

[BURHAN:v1p217/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · أبو عبيد القاسم بن سلام، أحمد بن يحيى ثعلب | reports | One view takes the seven ahruf as seven Arab tribal dialects distributed across the Qur'an, not seven alternatives for each word; the dialects differ while meanings remain the same.
[BURHAN:v1p217/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · الأزهري | reports | Al-Azhari calls this the preferred view and cites Uthman's instruction to write in Quraysh speech when he and Zayd disagreed, since most revelation came in that language.
[BURHAN:v1p217/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · البيهقي | reports | Al-Bayhaqi calls the dialect view correct, citing Ibn Masʿud's advice to read as taught without affected disputation, like synonymous commands; Ibn Sirin said similarly, and valid readings are confined to the agreed imam codex.
[BURHAN:v1p217/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari rebuts Ibn Qutayba's claim that no word has multiple readings by listing forms such as ʿabada al-taghut, yartaʿ wa-yalʿab, baʿid, and bāʾis.
[BURHAN:v1p217/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن عبد البر | rejects | Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr argues seven tribal languages would not have prompted companions to condemn one another's readings; ʿUmar and Hisham were both Quraysh yet differed, and ʿUmar challenged Hisham.

[BURHAN:v1p235/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · البيهقي | reports | Al-Bayhaqi says Abu Bakr first gathered the Qur'an in one codex; Uthman later copied it into multiple codices when reading disagreements threatened to spread.
[BURHAN:v1p235/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · زيد بن ثابت | reports | Zayd reports that arrangement occurred in the Prophet's lifetime, the codex collection under Abu Bakr, and copying into codices under Uthman, drawing on both written materials and companions' memorization.
[BURHAN:v1p235/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The work was done with consultation and approval of the companions; ʿAli approved Uthman's effort and praised its result.
[BURHAN:v1p235/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي أبو بكر | reports | Al-Baqillani says Uthman aimed to unify people on readings established from the Prophet and discard unsupported forms, not to perform Abu Bakr's initial collection.
[BURHAN:v1p235/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي أبو بكر | reports | The Uthmanic codex excluded additions, omissions, glosses, and abrogated recitations, to prevent later corruption and doubt.
[BURHAN:v1p235/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · أنس | reports | Anas's report in al-Bukhari says Hudhayfa, alarmed by Syrian-Iraqi recitation disputes during campaigns in Armenia and Azerbaijan, urged Uthman to act before divisions resembled those among Jews and Christians.
[BURHAN:v1p235/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · عثمان | reports | Uthman borrowed Hafsa's sheets and appointed Zayd with three Quraysh members to copy them, instructing the Quraysh members to choose Quraysh speech if they disagreed with Zayd.
[BURHAN:v1p235/r8] BURHAN, d. 794 · عثمان | reports | After copying, Uthman returned Hafsa's sheets, sent a codex to each region, and ordered other Qur'anic written materials burned.
[BURHAN:v1p251/r8] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The debt verse is longest at 128 words and 540 letters; al-Duha then al-Fajr are shortest. He rejects مدهامتان and ثم نظر as shorter candidates based on their letter or word counts.
[BURHAN:v1p253#2/r14] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | The verse on deferred debts contains thirty-three instances of the letter mīm.

[BURHAN:v1p332/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · شيخ المالكية | holds | The Maliki shaykh forbids anomalous readings in prayer or elsewhere, even for readers ignorant of Arabic; the uninformed are taught, while knowing or persistent readers are disciplined.
[BURHAN:v1p332/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · شيخ المالكية | holds | He says replacing Qur’anic words such as آتينا and سولت with synonyms is not a variant reading but an even graver offense, deserving stronger discipline and prohibition.
[BURHAN:v1p332/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | The Maliki shaykh prefers not to combine different canonical readings in one verse; combining forms where one reading depends on the other, including this phrase with فتذكر in the accusative, is prohibited under the same ruling.

[BURHAN:v1p332/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · الشيخ شهاب الدين | reports | Shihab al-Din dislikes repeatedly reciting a verse with different readings as some contemporaries do during a Qur’an completion, calling it an innovation without early precedent.
[BURHAN:v1p332/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · النووي عن أصحاب الشافعي | reports | Al-Nawawi reports the Shafi‘i jurists’ view that anomalous readings are not Qur’an because they lack mass transmission, so reciting them in prayer or elsewhere is forbidden.
[BURHAN:v1p332/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن عبد البر | reports | Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr transmits Muslim consensus that anomalous readings may not be recited and that one should not pray behind someone who uses them.
[BURHAN:v1p446/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | One proposed most hopeful verse is the debt passage: God’s care reaches even the recording of small debts, suggesting hope from such great concern for people. | mentions 2:282

[BURHAN:v1p481/r9] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي أبو بكر الباقلاني | reports | Al-Baqillani regards Qur'anic quotation in poetry as disliked; eloquence scholars permit it as a rhetorical figure, calling it tadmin in earlier usage and iqtibas later.
[BURHAN:v2p10/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The author lists Qur’anic denunciations as signs that an act is forbidden, including calling it injustice, wrongful appropriation, sin, or fisq, as in the ban on harming scribes and witnesses.
[BURHAN:v2p14/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | An absolute ruling is restricted by a qualified one when that is its only basis; examples include just witnesses, inheritances after bequest or debt, believing-slave expiation, ablution, and blood restricted to flowing blood.
[BURHAN:v2p206/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | prefers | The stronger reading is that a scribe or witness must not be harmed, including by concealing the writing or testimony; another reading forbids callers from burdening them at harmful times.
[BURHAN:v2p22/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Stating a qualification can distinguish a special case within its class even when omitted cases share the rule; the author gives several rhetorical benefits for such specification.
[BURHAN:v2p22/r8] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The fallback of one man and two women is another example in the discussion of specifying circumstances in a legal rule.

[BURHAN:v2p397/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari says debt is stated explicitly so the pronoun in write it has an antecedent.
[BURHAN:v2p397/r8] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | rejects | Zarkashi rejects that necessity because the implied verbal noun in contracting a debt could itself supply the antecedent for the pronoun.

[BURHAN:v2p438/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | In فإن لم يكونا رجلين, the dual witnesses are understood from the pronoun and the preceding شهيدين; رجلين can be read as a circumstantial phrase, as in وضعتها أنثى. | mentions 3:36

[BURHAN:v2p439/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · بعضهم | rejects | Some parse رجلين as an explanatory circumstantial accusative with complete kāna; the author says this answers a question about parsing, not the rhetorical arrangement, and adds needless strain.
[BURHAN:v2p439/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | prefers | The author’s preferred reading takes شهيدين as two witnesses of either sex, then qualifies them as men; the pronoun returns to the unqualified pair, so the condition negates their being men and fits the fallback.
[BURHAN:v2p484/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Names and the topic of a statement are normally explicit when first mentioned; a repeated name is usually replaced by a pronoun because the referent is already known.
[BURHAN:v2p484/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The first reason to repeat an explicit noun instead of using a pronoun is to magnify or honor it; examples include repeated mention of God, the Quran's dawn recitation, and Zechariah.
[BURHAN:v2p490/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Stating the one on whom reliance is placed strengthens the addressee's motive; repeating God's name in the next clause reinforces the appeal.
[BURHAN:v2p495/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Repeating إحداهما instead of using a pronoun gives the noun greater importance and balances the two clauses; the author calls this rare structural or semantic parallelism, beyond mere sound-patterning.
[BURHAN:v2p495/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · أبو الفتح عن المتنبي | reports | Al-Fath recounts asking al-Mutanabbi whether he wrote قرحى or قرحا; al-Mutanabbi chose the latter because the following بهارا is a plural, an example of deliberate balance in wording.
[BURHAN:v2p495/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The verse has parallel clauses for error and reminder; repeating the subject before the second action preserves its form and lets the clause close with balanced structure, while الأخرى clarifies the intended contrast.
[BURHAN:v2p501/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The verse's repeated explicit name of God exemplifies the broader preference for restating a noun when the intervening material is long or a new verse begins. | mentions 2:143, 24:35, 24:37

[BURHAN:v3p392/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The passage lists declarative forms such as God's counter-maneuver, His making mockery, and like-for-like recompense as wording placed where a demand or response is intended.

[BURHAN:v3p392/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The fourth kind negates a qualifier of the subject or object; in I saw no writing man, it may weakly imply seeing a nonwriter, while denying the seeing itself is another weak reading.

[BURHAN:v3p96/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · سيبويه والبصريون | reports | For this verse, neither “lest one err” nor “for fear of error” makes error a sensible purpose of testimony; the intended purpose is reminder if one forgets, with error as its trigger, like preparing a prop to support a wall if it leans.
[BURHAN:v4p142/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · أبو الفتح | reports | Abu al-Fath, from a Mu'tazili premise that human disobedience is not attributable to God, interpreted the form as meaning found rather than as causative.
[BURHAN:v4p142/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | rejects | The author rejects Abu al-Fath's interpretation as weak and says a verb's intransitive or reflexive counterpart need not be joined by fa.
[BURHAN:v4p142/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · بعض الناس | reports | Some infer that piety causes divine teaching from the juxtaposition of the two clauses.

[BURHAN:v4p24/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari composed two volumes on pronouns occurring in the Qur'an, with many discussions.

[NASHR:v1p387/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · author | reports | The differing-hamza class has one locus, من الشهداء أن, except for Hamza’s reading, as already noted in the two-kasra discussion.
[NASHR:v1p387/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | The fifth class has a ḍamma then kasra and 22 agreed occurrences, including ولا يأب الشهداء إذا and الفقراء إلى الله; six occurrences differ, including Maryam’s يا ذكرياء إنا and five addresses to the Prophet attributed to Nafi.
[NASHR:v1p387/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · author | prefers | For the fifth class, early authorities mostly replace the softened second hamza with a pure kasra waw; later authorities mostly use a between-between sound. Al-Dani says the latter is better by analogy, the former stronger in transmission.
[NASHR:v1p6/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو عبيد القاسم بن سلام | reports | Abū ʿUbayd lists Companion transmitters of reading forms: numerous Muhājirūn including Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, and Ibn Masʿūd, and Anṣār including Ubayy, Muʿādh, Zayd, and Anas.
[NASHR:v1p6/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو بكر الصديق | reports | After the Prophet’s death and the wars against apostates and Musaylima, in which about five hundred Companions were killed, Abū Bakr was urged to compile the Qurʾan lest it be lost with them; he first hesitated because the Prophet had not ordered it.
[NASHR:v1p6/r3] NASHR, d. 833 · زيد بن ثابت | reports | Abū Bakr and the Companions agreed to collection, and Zayd ibn Thābit gathered the Qurʾan into sheets kept successively by Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and Ḥafṣa.
[NASHR:v1p6/r4] NASHR, d. 833 · حذيفة بن اليمان | reports | Around 30 AH, Ḥudhayfa saw Muslims in Armenia and Azerbaijan disputing whose recitation was more correct and urged ʿUthmān to intervene before they divided like Jews and Christians.
[NASHR:v1p6/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · عثمان | reports | ʿUthmān borrowed Ḥafṣa’s sheets and appointed Zayd, Ibn al-Zubayr, Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith to copy them; in disagreement with Zayd, they were to write in Quraysh’s tongue because revelation came in it.
[NASHR:v1p6/r6] NASHR, d. 833 · عثمان | reports | ʿUthmān sent codices to Basra, Kufa, Syria, Mecca, Yemen, and Bahrain, left one in Medina, and kept the central copy for himself.
[NASHR:v1p6/r7] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | The community agreed on the contents of these codices and set aside divergent additions, omissions, and word substitutions that had been permitted but were not established by widespread transmission as Qurʾan.
[NASHR:v1p6/r8] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | The codices were left without dots or vowel marks so their script could accommodate sound transmitted readings; reliance was on memorization as well as the written outline.
[NASHR:v2p208/r4] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو عمرو والكسائي وأبو جعفر وقالون | reports | These readers silence the medial hāʾ of هو when it follows waw, fāʾ, or lām, as in وهو, فهو, لهو, وهي, فهي, and لهي; al-Kisai also does so in ثم هو.
[NASHR:v2p208/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abu Jaʿfar has both sukūn and ḍamma routes for the hāʾ in ثم هو and يمل هو; Ibn al-Jazari accepts both as sound.
[NASHR:v2p208/r6] NASHR, d. 833 · قالون | reports | Qalun likewise has both hāʾ forms in these two phrases, though the sukūn route is rare through Abu Nashit; Ibn al-Jazari read both through the cited routes.
[NASHR:v2p227/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · ابن كثير والبصريان | reports | Ibn Kathir and the two Basrans read the rāʾ with ḍamma; the other readers use fatḥa. The author gives no semantic distinction here.
[NASHR:v2p227/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abu Jaʿfar has two transmitted forms: some routes lighten and silence the rāʾ, while other routes double it with fatḥa; all retain the alif’s lengthening at the meeting of two sukūns.
[NASHR:v2p235/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · author | reports | Two Bazzī-related readings, known through Ibn Badahan alone from al-Zaynabi, were absent from the other authorities’ routes; al-Dani included them by textual analogy, and al-Shatibi followed, while this author includes them because they appear in the Taysir and Shatibiyya and fit the Bazzī rule.

[NASHR:v2p236/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · الباقون | reports | The other readers read the hamza in أن تضل with fatḥa.

[NASHR:v2p236/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · ابن كثير والبصريان | reports | Ibn Kathīr and the two Basran readers pronounce فتذكر without gemination.
[NASHR:v2p236/r6] NASHR, d. 833 · الباقون | reports | The other readers pronounce فتذكر with gemination.

[NASHR:v2p236/r8] NASHR, d. 833 · الباقون | reports | The other readers read both words in تجارة حاضرة in the nominative.

[BIQAI-FULL:v1p544#2/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Charity and avoiding usury purify wealth while principal remains lawful and insolvent debtors receive respite; this may tempt debtors to feign insolvency, so the debt verse teaches preservation through documentation.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p544#2/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Debt documentation is guidance rather than an obligation, modeled on Gods own recording of deeds by trustworthy angels and in a revealed book.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p544#2/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Tadayantum describes mutual dealings over debt; debt is a liability, whether due now or later, unlike present cash or goods.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p544#2/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The added phrase by debt excludes a sale of debt for debt, since that transaction would involve two debts.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p544#2/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | A debts deadline must be specified; an unknown term is invalid, and the appointment of a term hints at resurrection and fulfillment of Gods promise.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p544#2/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the conditional wording indicates that people will inevitably enter debt transactions.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p544#2/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Mention of an appointed term points toward resurrection, when the promise of fulfillment is realized.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p545/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Since most people cannot write, the directive to appoint a just scribe does not select one specific person.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p545/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The writer may be a child or slave, provided the writing is done fairly.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p545/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Just writing follows the model of Gods trustworthy recording angels. | mentions 82:10, 80:15
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p545/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | A writer should not refuse this recommended service; gratitude to God requires writing as He taught, without diminishing the record.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p545/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The debtor dictates the obligation so the scribe and those present can witness what is owed.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p545/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | A foolish debtor lacks sound judgment, so his admission is not treated as reliable; a weak person may be temporarily ill, young, old, or otherwise impaired.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p545/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Someone unable to dictate may be inarticulate, shy, or unable to speak Arabic; a guardian, trustee, judge, interpreter, or agent dictates fairly for that person.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p545/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The guardian must not wrong either the ward or creditor when speaking on the ward's behalf.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p545/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The debtor must fear God and avoid any shortfall; bakhs means a particularly severe reduction that wrongs the recipient.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p546/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali compares a guardian's tongue speaking for a ward with God's words recited by human tongues, and likens the ward's limited capacity to needing a guardian's mature ability. | mentions 1:5, 2:257
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p546/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Writing and testimony are not automatically linked, so the verse separately directs people to seek two witnesses, with the word shahid emphasizing established insight and experience.

-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali analogizes the two debt witnesses to reflection on visible signs and consideration of heard signs.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p546/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The phrase your men implies Muslim witnesses and, by the verse's wording and conditions, free witnesses; the witness must be reliable and accepted.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p546/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali sees the wording as broad accommodation for two women when two men cannot be found, while suggesting disagreement over cases where a man might be sought.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p546/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The two women must be among those whose uprightness is approved; testimony is penetrating perception of hidden meaning through an apparent form.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p546/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | One woman may lose or forget some testimony, so the other reminds her; the verse makes this the reason two women stand in place of one man.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p546/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the readings with light and doubled consonants distinguish women who forget once from those who repeatedly forget; either may forget different details, allowing mutual correction.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p547/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The reference to reminding implies that testimony without recall is barred; the verse also uses reciprocal omission, with one side understood from the other.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p547/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Witnesses should be present whenever parties trade, immediately or later, whether for business or another purpose; this instruction is guidance, not an obligation.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p547/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Witnesses must not refuse either to bear testimony when called or to give it after bearing it; the added ma makes the summons emphatic.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p547/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | People must not tire of documenting either small or large debts through their due date; the separate warning magnifies a duty people might neglect.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p547/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali explains small and large by each debtor's perception and means, rather than the absolute quantity that little and much would describe.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p547/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · ابن السيد | reports | Ibn al-Sayyid reports that qasata can mean either injustice or justice; here aqsatu means more equitable, preserving balance without shortchanging.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p547/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Written debts make evidence more upright and reduce doubt; the record can also settle men's uncertainty, just as mutual reminding addresses women's lapses.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p547/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The future term creates risk of forgetting, which explains the emphasis on writing; hand-to-hand trade is exempt because it is immediately exchanged and unlikely to be disputed.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p547/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | For immediate trade, Asim reads the phrase as an incomplete construction, while other readers use a complete verb; either way the trade is conducted among the parties.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p547/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The exemption from writing applies to cash trade, because merchandise circulates and is not held by one person for long.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p549/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The prohibition on harming a scribe or witness covers both causing harm and suffering harm; the author says both readings make sense.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p549/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the verse encourages kindness to scribes and witnesses and permits compensation when their work would otherwise damage their livelihood.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p549/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Breaking the prohibition is fisq, a departure from God's law; the emphatic form intensifies the warning.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p549/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The closing call to fear God addresses the stratagems by which traders pursue private advantage, while promising teaching and warning of threat.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p549/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali takes the enduring form teaches to promise continued divine instruction beyond what people can reach through this guidance alone.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p561/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-Baqara spans relations between God and people through religion, between people through transactions and conflicts, and within the self through faith and covenants.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p563/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | The debt guidance cultivates trust in God and support from Him; the Prophet died practicing it, and the surah's final movement emphasizes faith and reliance on the King of Kings in jihad.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p563/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali divides the surah into three parts, each with a foundation and warning at its close, while the final part receives added emphasis as the completion.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p564/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The promise that God teaches those who fear Him supports the preceding point about expanded understanding of Qur'anic knowledge. | mentions 2:282

[DURR-FULL:v2p115/r8] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib says it reached him that the debt verse was the last Qur'anic verse with the Throne.
[DURR-FULL:v2p115/r9] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن شهاب | reports | Ibn Shihab says the last Qur'anic material with the Throne was the usury verse and the debt verse.
[DURR-FULL:v2p117/r1] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas affirms that deferred advance sales to a specified term are authorized by God, citing the debt verse.

[DURR-FULL:v2p117/r5] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Debt should be witnessed to prevent denial or forgetting; someone who refuses a needed request to testify despite holding evidence disobeys, while a requester must not burden a scribe or witness when another is available.

[BURSEVI:v1p359#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The stated due date should use days, months, years, or another precise measure; harvest, threshing, or a pilgrim’s arrival are too uncertain.
[BURSEVI:v1p359#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Writing the debt and its due date is safer and prevents disputes; the majority consider the command a recommendation.
[BURSEVI:v1p359#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The scribe should mediate between both parties and record what each says, in equal terms without favor, addition, or omission; they should choose a learned, religious jurist whose document is legally reliable.
[BURSEVI:v1p359#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | A scribe should not refuse to write the debt in the manner God taught for documenting agreements; the command reinforces the preceding prohibition.
[BURSEVI:v1p359#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The debtor should dictate because he is the party answerable and must acknowledge the obligation.
[BURSEVI:v1p359#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The debtor is especially warned to fear God and not reduce the dictated amount, since self-protection gives him an incentive to understate what he owes.
[BURSEVI:v1p359#3/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | A person unable to dictate may also be hindered by ignorance or another impediment; a guardian then takes over.
[BURSEVI:v1p359#3/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The person’s guardian, administrator, proxy, or translator dictates fairly, without increasing or reducing the amount.
[BURSEVI:v1p359#3/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Two male witnesses are sought to carry testimony about the transaction; they are called witnesses in anticipation of giving testimony later.
[BURSEVI:v1p359#3/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | ‘From your men’ means free adult Muslims of your community; in transactions between unbelievers or where the debtor is an unbeliever, unbelievers may be witnesses according to the author’s school.
[BURSEVI:v1p359#3/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may witness financial matters by consensus; women do not testify in fixed punishments or retaliation, where men are required.
[BURSEVI:v1p359#3/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The requirement that witnesses be approved applies to both the man and the women; women are included by grammatical predominance, and the phrase points to trust and known integrity.
[BURSEVI:v1p360#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | If active, the prohibition bars a scribe from refusing or altering the document and a witness from withholding testimony; if passive, it bars others from harming them while occupied or withholding their fee.
[BURSEVI:v1p360#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Violating the ban on harm is disobedience; believers should fear God in all His commands and prohibitions, and He teaches rulings that serve their interests and knows their conduct.
[BURSEVI:v1p360#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The verse’s detailed protection of people’s rights shows that safeguarding property is necessary; those who pursue truth are saved, while others stray.
[BURSEVI:v1p360#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God teaches transaction rules out of mercy to prevent injustice, quarrels, resentment, and worldly distress; this shows that religious obligations also bring purification and blessing. | mentions 5:6
[BURSEVI:v1p360#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The first of three lessons concerns God’s relation to servants: His care in worldly dealings prevents loss and dispute and indicates that religious duties likewise express mercy and bring His blessings. | mentions 5:6
[BURSEVI:v1p360/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | One woman may forget and the other remind her; reminder is the real purpose, while possible error is named as its cause, as in preparing a weapon to repel a possible enemy.
[BURSEVI:v1p360/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Witnesses should not refuse when summoned to give or bear testimony.
[BURSEVI:v1p360/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Do not tire of documenting a debt, large or small, whether summarized or detailed, through its agreed due date.
[BURSEVI:v1p360/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Documenting it to the due date is fairest before God, strengthens testimony, and best prevents doubt about the debt, amount, term, or witnesses.
[BURSEVI:v1p360/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Immediate exchange with both parties present may be left unwritten because hand-to-hand trade is less prone to dispute and forgetting.
[BURSEVI:v1p360/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Witness sales either in this particular transaction or generally as a precaution; the majority take the verse’s commands as recommendations.
[BURSEVI:v1p361#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God knows hidden thoughts and secrets and rewards people according to the sincerity and purity of their intentions; blessed is the person who purifies his character and seeks the unseen.
[BURSEVI:v1p361#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | A Persian poem compares the unseen to a decorated palace and desire to a cloud of dust: abandoning desire removes the screen and enables sight of the desired reality.
[BURSEVI:v1p361/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The second lesson concerns servants’ relation to God: carefulness over fleeting worldly transactions should teach even greater care over enduring afterlife matters, for every atom of good and evil is rewarded or punished.
[BURSEVI:v1p361/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God’s covenant with believers is a purchase of their lives and property for Paradise, witnessed by the angels; the written contract records a jewel from Paradise deposited as the Black Stone.

[ALUSI-FULL:v3p60/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Saʾama means to tire of or become annoyed by something; the verse discourages weariness over recording debt.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p61/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | God knows every matter and will repay people for their conduct.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p61/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Repeating the divine name in three successive independent clauses is laudable when it magnifies the subject; here the clauses exhort piety, promise divine instruction, and glorify God’s knowledge.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p61/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The clauses differ as exhortation, promise, and declaration, which explains their connective pattern; treating the middle clause as a circumstantial clause is possible but less preferred.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He defines imlāl as dictating from memory and infers that the debtor should propose and dictate the written debt record.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Witness competence requires sound retention; witnesses lacking moral probity or reliable acquisition or retention of evidence are not admissible.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A witness need not remember the event continuously, provided they can properly recall it when giving testimony.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Someone who recorded an event, later forgot it, and then recalls it clearly by consulting the record may testify.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Someone who only knows they made a record but still cannot recall the event must not testify.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Witnesses should not be prompted; one who has forgotten should be able to remember independently.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Requiring at least two witnesses removes suspicion and the possibility of error or forgetfulness, displaying the strength of their retention and justice.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He generalizes that women’s retention is weaker and forgetfulness more likely than men’s, while allowing individual exceptions and treating gender and the majority as the legal reference.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He attributes women’s alleged forgetfulness partly to greater sensitivity and emotional impressions, which can weaken recall even in intelligent people.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r18] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He says women are more inwardly oriented and less engaged with external affairs such as commerce and debts, which he regards as primarily men’s work.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r19] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He says modesty and reserve predominate in women and should do so, and that even a small engagement diminishes their distinct worth and leaves fewer reminders of events.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | While dictating, the debtor must fear God rather than the scribe and must not reduce any part of the creditor’s right.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r20] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He calls a woman’s becoming manlike a degradation and says both feminized men’s and masculinized women’s testimony is inadmissible because they depart from their sex-specific perfection and may distort truth.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r21] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He treats women’s comparatively lower retention of external events as a consequence of their sex-specific nature, while saying a woman who later recalls an event fully can testify.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r22] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | It is unjust to compel women to record events or, after a human lapse of memory, to make them recover recollection through outside prompts.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r23] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Two women can confer before testifying and remind one another without outside prompting, strengthening their recall and preserving both their dignity and the right entrusted to them.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r24] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | If neither woman forgot, their evidentiary position is stronger; the mutual reminder need not happen in court, where it could prevent acceptance of testimony.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r25] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Where men can know the matter, women should not be made witnesses; if no man is available and a woman must be called, two women should serve for one man.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r26] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | For matters men cannot witness, women’s reports alone may suffice, sometimes even one woman’s report, as with an incident in a women’s bath or a midwife’s report of birth.

[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A debtor unable to dictate includes a spendthrift fool, a minor or mentally deficient person, or anyone unable because of muteness, stammering, ignorance,

[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The debtor’s guardian, trustee, agent, translator, or the creditor as debt-holder may dictate in the debtor’s place, fairly and justly.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The wording “your men” excludes children and non-Muslim men’s testimony against Muslims as sufficient testimony.
[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The witnesses must be people whose testimony is accepted and whose justice and reliability are known; a random pairing is not valid.

[ELMALILI:2:282#2/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | On Hamza’s reading, if one woman forgets or errs, the other reminds her.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A summons to bear or give testimony must not be refused: testimony is a collective duty, and becomes individually obligatory when nobody else can meet the need or particular people are required.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The exception is a fully cash, hand-to-hand commercial transaction; in that case leaving it unwritten causes no blame.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Even a cash sale may be written privately or in a short memorandum, though the burden on people who cannot write may outweigh the benefit.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | For any sale, including a cash sale, make it openly in the presence of witnesses rather than secretly; this precaution protects property and legal security.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | The majority of exegetes regard witnessing a sale here as a recommendation for precaution.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | The command not to harm a scribe or witness can mean they must not harm rights-holders by refusing a request or falsifying or altering the writing or testimony.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Alternatively, on the passive reading, scribes and witnesses themselves must not be harmed by excessive demands, interruption of important work, or denial of a scribe’s fee.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Causing such harm is a transgression against God’s obedience.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God will teach people more knowledge and rulings that serve their welfare.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r18] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Because God knows everything, believers should obey commands, avoid prohibitions, trust His promise, honor Him, and secure their dealings; piety is the foundation of that security.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Some scholars restrict the prohibition to accepting testimony, others to giving it, and many choose the latter; the author follows the view that the wording is unrestricted and includes both.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Qatada relates that the verse was revealed after a man went from camp to camp seeking a witness and no one paid attention.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Although giving testimony is especially important, necessity can make both accepting and giving testimony individually obligatory.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Every debt, large or small, should be documented in detail through its due date, including all particulars and qualities, rather than dismissed as too minor to write.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Some read the command to keep writing as an explanation and emphasis of the earlier command, directed to scribes; the author finds the broader contextual reading more fitting.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | He prefers understanding the command to address both parties, scribes, and witnesses, urging them to keep their own records and, where possible, write down testimony they have undertaken.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Detailed documentation has three benefits: it is most just before God, supports the establishment of testimony, and most nearly prevents doubt.
[ELMALILI:2:282#3/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A complete record secures confidence about the debt’s kind, amount, term, witnesses, testimony, and the parties’ moral, legal, and social relations.
[ELMALILI:2:282/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | The verse's readings differ on the forms of an tadilla and fa-tudhakkira; Hamza reads with the hamza's kasra, while Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and Yaqub use a still zā and an ungeminated kāf.
[ELMALILI:2:282/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Appointing legal document scribes is among the government's duties, and such scribes must write when asked.
[ELMALILI:2:282/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The debtor dictates the note because its contents constitute the debtor's acknowledgment and the witness statement is against that party.
[ELMALILI:2:282/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Hamza also reads the relevant form with rāʾ in the nominative, whereas readings other than Asim's use the nominative for wa-la yudārra.
[ELMALILI:2:282/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Abu Jaafar reads tijāratan hāḍiratan with an ungeminated rāʾ; Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read furuhun with both rāʾ and hāʾ vocalized and without the alif.
[ELMALILI:2:282/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Called the Verse of Debt, this is the Quran's longest verse.
[ELMALILI:2:282/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | One report gives the occasion of revelation as salam, paying in advance for goods delivered later, though the ruling covers every kind of sale and debt transaction.
[ELMALILI:2:282/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Linguists distinguish a loan from debt, so the verse's condition need not cover a pure loan; jurisprudence treats a loan first as a trust and finally as a currency exchange, with no fixed repayment date.
[ELMALILI:2:282/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Any debt transaction with a specified, known due date should be written; credit trading remains permissible despite the ban on usury, provided the due date is known and documented.
[ELMALILI:2:282/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A neutral scribe should record both parties' rights equally; parties may keep private records, but those do not replace the impartial written contract.
[ELMALILI:2:282/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A scribe must write as God taught, following proper documentary practice, justice, or gratitude for the gift of literacy; writing is a collective duty that becomes an individual duty when assigned.
[ELMALILI:v1p89/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Fuzûlî | reports | Fuzuli curses scribes who ruin fine writing; his Arabic stanza opens with a deliberate echo of the 'tabbat yada' wording.
[ELMALILI:v1p89/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A prose rendering conveys the Arabic stanza's sense—bad scribes ruin a work founded on learning and adab and spoil copies—but cannot equal the poem's effect.
[ELMALILI:v1p89/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Although literally translated, the prose version lacks the original's rhythmic harmony and cannot be offered as a proverb in the same way.
[ELMALILI:v1p89/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Fuzuli's Turkish version is not identical in content but expresses an equivalent idea and preserves literary value by supplying features absent from the Arabic wording.
[ELMALILI:v1p89/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The changes from ʿineb to ʿayb, ṣūr to shūr, nādir to nār, and göz to kör all exemplify corruption through altered letters or dots.
[ELMALILI:v1p89/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The Turkish rendering is an analogous poetic imitation rather than a literal translation; Elmalılı says this is the only way to translate literary works equivalently.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A human trying to compose a medium-length sura would need prolonged revision and still leave awkward sentences; the Quran’s fluent composition entails no such labor.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The Quran encourages extended recitation; Ibn Ashur reads ما تيسر as reciting as much as one can manage, with coherence and stylistic variety helping sustain it. | mentions 73:20
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أبو بكر بن العربي | reports | In Siraj al-Muridin, Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi calls the links among Quranic verses a great science, making them cohere like a single phrase.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r13] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · فخر الدين الرازي | reports | Al-Razi says the Quran is inimitable through arrangement and verse order as well as eloquent wording and noble meanings; al-Isfahani suggests this is what style-based claims mean.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r14] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Rhetoric extends beyond the states of verbal syntax to the ways in which those structures deliver meaning.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Quranic prose uses balanced, near-rhyming endings without rhetorical necessity or the constraints of meter, giving it smooth and harmonious delivery.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The Quran’s prose form itself contributes to its inimitability; it gathers known Arabic styles and innovates new ones.

1p115/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Stylistic variety shows divine origin because literary geniuses usually excel in only one or two styles, and intensifies the challenge by denying opponents the excuse that they had not tried a given style.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A distinctive Quranic style combines exhortation and legislation: its apparent wording teaches listeners what they need, while its depths yield many legal and ethical rulings to learned readers.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur cites the statement that only God and those firmly grounded in knowledge know its interpretation as an example of the Quran’s layered meanings and allusions to causes and purposes. | mentions 3:7
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur calls tafannun the artful movement between topics through parenthesis, analogy, conclusion, varied synonyms, and frequent grammatical shifts, before returning to the main subject and renewing attention.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The two parables of hypocrites, the fire and the rainstorm, exemplify this movement between styles and topics. | mentions 2:17, 2:18, 2:19, 2:20
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p115/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Transitions are finely connected and barely noticed, holding listeners’ attention and relieving the weariness of extended recitation.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p128/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | This scholarly dimension of inimitability belongs to the Quran as a whole, not every verse or sura separately; the challenge is only alluded to in the challenge to inconsistency. | mentions 4:82
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p128/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | For Arabs, the Quran’s sciences were inaccessible before its revelation; Ibn Ashur cites the statement that neither Muhammad nor his people knew them beforehand. | mentions 11:49
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p128/r12] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | For the general public, the miracle is that such knowledge came through a man raised unlettered among an unlettered people.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p128/r13] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | For People of the Book, the Quran reports their religious knowledge through an unlettered Prophet distant from their communities, abrogates their religions, and denounces their distortions; had he learned from them, they would have exposed it.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p128/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الشاطبي | reports | Al-Shatibi says Quranic meanings and interpretation must stay within what is customary among Arabs.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p128/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The authentic report says every prophet received signs that people believed because of, while Muhammad’s gift was revelation and he hoped for the greatest following.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p128/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur reads آمن عليه as believing because of the sign and according to its terms: each prophet’s miracle addressed a field especially admired and beyond his people.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p56/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · جماعة منهم أبو بكر الباقلائي وابن عبد البر وأبو بكر بن العربي والطبري والطحاوي | reports | Al-Baqillani, Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn al-Arabi, al-Tabari, and al-Tahawi, with this view attributed to Ibn Uyayna and Ibn Wahb, hold that the seven-letter license was later abrogated after allowing tribal dialects.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p56/r15] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | rejects | Ibn Ashur rejects that categorical account as mismatched with the hadith’s transmitted context of concession and ease, and says its forced sevenfold classifications do not withstand objection.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p56/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجمهور | reports | One explanation makes the seven letters synonymous expressions conveying one meaning, a concession letting reciters use whichever synonym comes readily to ease recitation.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p98/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Adding bi-dayn may be emphatic, or it may provide the noun resumed by write it; al-Zamakhshari says it also makes clear the distinction between deferred and immediate debts.
